title: Senior staff engineers win by asking the right question early
body: The final chapter of the handbook is about judgment: how a senior staff storage engineer thinks when someone says 'we need to store this'. Such an engineer is rarely the person who knows the most internals. Their value is asking the right question early, before a wrong default gets baked into a hundred services and becomes nearly impossible to undo. The chapter packages that judgment as six mental models, a way to choose storage, a design-doc checklist, review questions, a trade-off catalog, and practice interview problems.
deeper:
The framing builds on the rest of the book. The first twelve chapters taught individual systems: media, file systems, engines, replication, erasure coding, and security. Chapter 13 showed how real companies such as Google, Meta, Amazon, Dropbox and Uber assembled those systems and later migrated them. Chapter 14 shifts from what systems do to how you decide.

Why does timing matter so much in storage? Bytes outlive code. A service can be rewritten in a quarter, but data written in a bad format, with no owner, no deletion path, or the wrong partition key sits on disk for years and must be migrated, not just redeployed. Every decision that is cheap on day one, such as choosing a retention default, emitting change data capture, or picking an open format, becomes a multi-month project in year three. So the senior staff skill is less about deep internals and more about spotting which early choice will be expensive later, and raising it while it is still a one-line change.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter say a senior staff engineer's key skill is asking the right question early rather than knowing the most internals?
quiz.a: Because storage mistakes persist: once a wrong default spreads across many services and data is on disk, fixing it means a slow migration instead of a cheap early change.

title: Data has a temperature: hot, warm, cold, frozen
body: Data has a lifecycle: it is born, used a lot, used less, then archived or deleted. How often it is read is its temperature. Hot data is read many times per second, warm data sometimes, cold data rarely but kept for a reason, and frozen data only for law or insurance. For most user content, access drops sharply with age, so storing everything on the fastest, most expensive media wastes money. Matching storage tier to temperature is the first lever for cost.
deeper:
The evidence comes from the big operators. Meta's f4 paper showed that photo read rates fall quickly after upload, which is why Meta built a separate warm tier alongside its hot Haystack store (Chapters 3 and 7). Google's Colossus places new data on flash and moves it to bigger disks as it cools (Chapter 13). Both designs follow the same curve: a short hot period, then a long tail of rare reads.

In practice you measure temperature, not guess it. Plot read rate against age at 1 day, 30 days and 1 year; the knee of that curve tells you when to move data. Temperature also interacts with redundancy choices later in the chapter: hot data is usually replicated for fast reads, while warm and cold data is erasure-coded to save bytes. Frozen data often lives in archival tiers with slow retrieval, which is fine because the only reader may be an auditor or a lawyer years later.

quiz.q: Why does storing all user content on the fastest tier waste money for most applications?
quiz.a: Access drops sharply with age, so most bytes quickly become warm or cold; paying hot-tier prices for rarely read data buys performance nobody uses.

title: Every tier boundary is a move, and every move can lose data
body: Tiering saves bytes, but each boundary between tiers is a data move, and every move is a chance to lose or duplicate data. Too many tiers cost more in operations than they save in storage. So the right question is not 'how many tiers can we have' but 'what does the read rate look like at 1 day, 30 days and 1 year, what is the retention rule, and who deletes it'. If nobody can answer who deletes it, the data will be kept forever and paid for forever.
deeper:
The trade-off is operational. Each tier needs a mover process, verification that the copy landed before the source is removed, handling for objects mutated or deleted mid-move, monitoring, and on-call knowledge. A two- or three-tier design is usually enough; adding a fifth tier to shave a few percent of cost can create more incidents than savings.

The 'who deletes it' question is the sharpest one in the model. Retention is a policy decision that needs an owner. Without one, the default becomes infinite retention, which the chapter later lists as the anti-pattern 'retention by nobody': the dataset grows until it becomes a cost incident or a compliance incident. Asking about deletion on day one forces a team to name a retention rule and an owner while the dataset is still small and the decision is cheap. Later in the chapter, the design-doc checklist includes a Lifecycle section covering temperature over time, tiering rules, TTLs, archival and deletion for exactly this reason.

quiz.q: What is the risk if nobody on a team can answer 'who deletes this data?'
quiz.a: The data is kept forever by default, so storage cost grows without limit and compliance risk rises; nobody owns the cleanup.

title: Durability is a repair-speed problem, not a copy-count problem
body: You lose data only when too many copies or fragments fail before the first failure is repaired. So durability depends less on how many copies you keep and more on how fast you rebuild a lost one. With three replicas, data is lost only if the other two fail during the repair window. That probability is roughly proportional to (repair time / disk lifetime) squared, so halving repair time cuts loss probability about fourfold. For an erasure code tolerating m failures, the effect scales roughly to the power m.
deeper:
The model assumes disks fail independently with an annualized failure rate (AFR), the fraction of devices expected to fail in a year, of about 1 to 2 percent. The chapter labels this an assumption and points to Backblaze's public drive statistics for real numbers.

The squared term is the key insight. For 3-way replication, after one disk dies, you need two more specific failures inside the repair window. Each is proportional to window length, so the joint chance scales with window squared. A code that survives m failures needs m more failures in the window, so shrinking the window pays off to the power m. This is why mean time to repair (MTTR) is a first-class design metric.

Chapter 10 stressed parallel repair for this reason. Dropbox's Magic Pocket spreads reconstruction across hundreds of storage nodes at once instead of copying to one replacement disk, and repair starts after a node has been offline for 15 minutes. Many sources feeding many destinations turns a days-long rebuild into a much shorter one.

quiz.q: Why does halving repair time improve durability roughly fourfold for 3-way replication?
quiz.a: Loss requires the other two replicas to fail during the repair window; that probability scales with the window squared, so half the window gives about a quarter of the risk.

title: Fast repair steals bandwidth from users, so throttle it carefully
body: Repair is not free. Rebuilding a lost disk or node reads and writes large amounts of data over the same network links and disks that serve user requests. If repair runs flat out, user latency suffers. If repair is throttled too hard, the repair window grows, and because loss probability scales with the window squared or higher, durability drops quickly. So repair traffic must be rate-limited, but not so much that the window stretches out.
deeper:
This is a classic tension a senior engineer must quantify rather than guess. The durability model says window length matters enormously; the performance model says background traffic hurts tail latency. The answer is usually a priority scheme: repair runs at a guaranteed minimum rate so the window stays bounded, and can burst when user load is light.

Parallelism softens the trade-off. When reconstruction is spread across hundreds of nodes, as in Dropbox's Magic Pocket, each node contributes only a small slice of bandwidth, so no single disk or link is saturated while the total repair rate stays high. Magic Pocket also waits until a node has been offline for 15 minutes before starting repair, which avoids wasting bandwidth rebuilding data for a machine that is only rebooting. That delay is itself a trade-off: a longer wait saves needless repairs but adds to the exposure window for real failures.

quiz.q: Why can't a storage system simply run repair at maximum speed to maximize durability?
quiz.a: Repair shares network and disk bandwidth with user traffic; running it flat out hurts user latency, so it must be rate-limited without letting the repair window grow too long.

title: RS(10,4): 1.4x overhead, survives 4 failures, but repair reads 10
body: Reed-Solomon RS(10,4) splits data into 10 data fragments plus 4 parity fragments, storing 14 in total. That is 1.4x storage overhead versus 3x for triple replication, and it tolerates 4 failures instead of 2. The catch is repair: rebuilding one lost fragment requires reading 10 fragments. That repair cost is why Azure invented Local Reconstruction Codes (LRC), and why hot data is often replicated while cold data is erasure-coded.
deeper:
Erasure coding in general splits data into k data and m parity fragments so that any k fragments can rebuild the original. Reed-Solomon is the classic code used by many storage systems.

The back-of-envelope math shows why it is attractive at scale: going from 3x to 1.4x overhead cuts raw storage by more than half for the same logical data, while improving failure tolerance. But three costs come with it. Writes need CPU to compute parity and network to spread 14 fragments across failure domains. Small reads may touch fragments on several nodes, adding latency. And repair amplifies I/O tenfold, which collides with the repair-speed model: slow, expensive repair enlarges the vulnerability window.

Azure's answer, covered in Chapter 13, was LRC: erasure codes with cheaper single-fragment repairs, because most failures are single failures. The practical rule the chapter draws is temperature-based: replicate hot, small, latency-sensitive data; erasure-code warm or cold, large objects where cost matters.

quiz.q: When would you choose erasure coding over replication, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: For warm or cold, large, immutable data where cost matters. It costs more CPU and network on write, higher latency for small reads, and more reads during repair.

title: Bytes scale by adding disks; metadata is what actually breaks
body: Storing bytes is easy to scale: add disks. Knowing where each byte is, who owns it and what it is called is hard to scale. Google's GFS hit limits because one master held all metadata in memory, and HDFS hit the same limit with its NameNode. Both Google and Meta solved it the same way: Colossus stores metadata in Bigtable and Tectonic stores it in ZippyDB, a sharded key-value store. Metadata, not capacity, is usually the first bottleneck in large storage systems.
deeper:
Metadata is data about data: names, sizes, locations and permissions. A single-master design is simple and works well at small scale, which is why GFS and HDFS started there. But every file costs memory on that one machine, and every open, list, rename and stat hits it. As file counts grow into the billions, the master runs out of RAM or request capacity long before the disks fill up.

The fix at Google and Meta was to treat metadata itself as a scalable database problem: shard it across a replicated key-value store (Bigtable for Colossus, ZippyDB for Tectonic), covered in Chapters 2 and 13. The trade-off catalog later frames this choice as central master versus sharded metadata store: pick a central master for small scale and simplicity, a sharded store for billions of files. The interview problem on a billion-file metadata service applies the same pattern, separating the namespace from block locations and sharding directories by hash of parent ID.

quiz.q: Why did both GFS and HDFS hit scaling limits even though they could add more disks?
quiz.a: Each used one master (GFS master, HDFS NameNode) holding all metadata in memory, so file count and metadata operations overwhelmed that single machine before capacity ran out.

title: Count objects, not bytes: small files kill byte-sized systems
body: A system sized by bytes can still collapse under object count. A million 1 KB files cost far more metadata than one 1 GB file, even though the bytes are similar. So when reviewing a design, ask how many objects, not just how many bytes. Ask what the metadata operation rate is for list, rename and stat, and which operation is O(number of files). Any operation whose cost grows with file count is a future outage.
deeper:
Each object carries fixed overhead: a metadata entry, a location record, often a per-request charge in cloud object stores, and work for LIST, replication and garbage collection. With tiny objects that overhead dominates the actual data.

The chapter's check-your-understanding question makes this concrete: a team plans to store 5 billion 2 KB records as separate objects in an object store. The main risk is metadata and per-object overhead: object count, LIST cost and per-request cost dominate. The fixes are to pack small records into larger files, which was Haystack's idea for photos, or to use a key-value store designed for small items instead.

The design-review questions echo this: 'Does anything scale with the number of files rather than bytes?' and 'Which resource runs out first: IOPS, capacity, CPU, memory, or metadata?' The Part 2 modifier table says it directly: object count drives metadata design, while bytes drive cost and tiering.

quiz.q: A team plans to store 5 billion 2 KB records as separate objects in an object store. What is the main risk and a fix?
quiz.a: Metadata and per-object overhead: object count, LIST cost and per-request cost dominate. Pack records into larger files or use a key-value store.

title: Blast radius: split into cells and stamps so one failure stays small
body: Blast radius is how much breaks when one thing breaks. Good designs limit it by splitting the system into independent units: cells, stamps, shards or regions. AWS uses cell-based architecture, where each cell is an independent copy of a service stack serving a subset of users. Azure uses storage stamps, fixed-size storage cluster units. In both, a bad deploy or a hot tenant affects only one slice, not every customer at once.
deeper:
The idea is containment. If every customer shares one giant cluster, a single bad configuration push, a runaway tenant, or a software bug can take everyone down together. If customers are spread across many independent cells, the same event hits only the users in that cell, and the rollout can be stopped before it spreads to others.

The unit of isolation varies. AWS cells are full service stacks; Azure stamps are fixed-size storage clusters (Chapters 10 and 13). Shards and regions are coarser or finer versions of the same principle. Deployments are typically rolled out cell by cell, so a bad release is caught in one unit.

The design-review question 'What is the blast radius of one bad deploy?' tests exactly this. A good answer names the unit and its size, such as 'one stamp, about N percent of customers', rather than 'we will be careful'. Blast radius is also one axis of the trade-off catalog, set against stranded capacity.

quiz.q: How do AWS cells and Azure stamps reduce the impact of a bad deploy?
quiz.a: Each is an independent unit serving a subset of users, so a bad deploy or hot tenant affects only that slice instead of the whole service.

title: Small cells bound failure but strand capacity: Meta vs Azure
body: Splitting into small units has a price. Each small unit needs its own headroom, so capacity is wasted, and units need rebalancing as load shifts. Big units pool resources better but fail bigger. Meta chose big Tectonic clusters to fix stranded capacity, meaning resources that exist but cannot be used by the workloads that need them. Azure chose stamps to bound failure. The chapter says both are right for their constraints: the choice depends on which risk dominates.
deeper:
Stranded capacity arises when free disk or IOPS sits in one unit while another unit is full. With many small cells, the sum of every cell's safety margin can be a large fraction of the fleet. Meta's Tectonic consolidated many separate storage systems into large shared clusters precisely so that spare capacity could be used by whichever tenant needed it.

Azure made the opposite call. Stamps are fixed-size, and the design-doc checklist cites Azure stamps staying under 70 percent utilization as a headroom target. That leaves capacity idle by design, but guarantees that a failure or overload inside one stamp cannot spread.

The trade-off catalog formalizes this: pick small cells or stamps when blast radius is the top risk; pick a giant shared pool when stranded capacity is the top cost. A shared pool then needs other protections, such as per-tenant quotas and priority classes, which the anti-pattern list says Tectonic provides through traffic classes.

quiz.q: Why did Meta choose large Tectonic clusters while Azure chose fixed-size stamps?
quiz.a: Meta's top concern was stranded capacity, which big pools fix; Azure prioritized bounding failure, which small units do. Each chose for its dominant risk.

title: The default is the policy: most teams never change it
body: Whatever a platform does by default, most teams will keep. So the default effectively is the policy. If default retention is 'forever', storage grows forever. If default replication is cross-region, cost doubles for data that never needed it. AWS made encryption at rest the S3 default in 2023, and after that nobody has to remember it. A senior staff engineer spends more time on defaults than on edge cases, asking: what happens if the team does nothing, and is that safe and cheap?
deeper:
The reasoning is behavioral. Teams are busy, and a platform setting that requires an explicit choice will be left alone by most of them. A default therefore applies to the majority of data in the company, while any carefully designed edge case might apply to one team.

That makes defaults high-leverage in both directions. A bad default silently multiplies cost or risk across every dataset: infinite retention accumulates personal data and bills, and cross-region synchronous replication by default makes every write pay a round trip (both appear later as anti-patterns). A good default removes a whole class of mistakes. The S3 example from 2023 is the model: once encryption at rest became automatic, there was no longer a checklist item anyone could forget (Chapter 11).

The key-takeaway version is: defaults are policy, so make the safe, cheap choice the one teams get by doing nothing. The review question 'What does the default retention cost in 3 years?' puts a number on it.

quiz.q: Why is 'retention: forever' a dangerous default?
quiz.a: Storage and cost grow without limit, compliance risk grows with every extra year of personal data, and nobody owns the cleanup.

title: Everything will be migrated within 5 to 10 years
body: Every storage system you choose today will be replaced within 5 to 10 years. The chapter lists examples from Chapter 13: Meta replaced Haystack and f4 with Tectonic, Amazon retail left Oracle, Uber is moving its data lake to the cloud, and Dropbox left S3 for its own Magic Pocket. Migration is not a failure of the original design; it is the normal lifecycle. So a good storage design plans for its own exit from the beginning.
deeper:
Why is migration inevitable? Scale changes by orders of magnitude, costs shift, new hardware arrives, vendors change pricing, and organizational priorities move. A system perfect for year one is rarely perfect for year eight.

The examples cover every direction: from specialized in-house stores to a unified one (Meta), from a commercial database to in-house services (Amazon retail), from on-premises to cloud (Uber), and from cloud to in-house (Dropbox). No choice is permanent.

The consequence is that 'how hard would it be to leave' is a real cost that should be priced during design, not discovered later. The chapter's interview problem on migrating 50 PB shows how long this takes: at 100 Gbps sustained, 50 PB needs about 46 days of pure transfer, so realistic migrations run for months. Designs that anticipated migration, with a routing layer, change streams and versioned records, make those months far less risky.

quiz.q: What is the practical implication of the claim that every storage system will be migrated within 5 to 10 years?
quiz.a: Design for the exit from day one, because the cost of leaving is a real, eventual cost that should be priced during design rather than discovered later.

title: Four day-one choices that make future migrations cheap
body: To design for migration, the chapter recommends four habits. Put an abstraction layer or stable API between applications and the storage engine, as Netflix did with its key-value layer. Emit change data capture (CDC), a stream of every change made to a database, from day one so a new store can be filled and kept in sync. Keep data in open formats such as Parquet and Iceberg where possible. And make every record carry a version or timestamp so dual writes and backfills can be reconciled.
deeper:
Each habit removes a specific migration pain. The abstraction layer means applications never talk to the engine directly, so the engine can be swapped behind the API without touching hundreds of callers; Netflix's KV data abstraction layer (2024) is the cited example.

CDC gives the new store a live feed. You backfill historical data, then replay the change stream so the new system stays current until cutover, instead of freezing writes.

Open formats mean the next engine can read existing files directly. The trade-off catalog notes proprietary formats allow deep optimization for one engine, but open formats win when many engines or future migrations matter; the anti-pattern list warns that proprietary formats for long-lived data turn the next migration into a full rewrite.

Versions or timestamps on every record let you resolve conflicts when both old and new systems receive writes, or when a backfilled copy races a fresh update: the newer version wins deterministically.

quiz.q: Name two ways to make a future migration cheaper, decided on day one.
quiz.a: Any two of: put a stable API or abstraction layer in front of the store; emit CDC; store data in open formats; version every record.

title: Senior staff lens: ask 'how would we leave this system?'
body: In a design review, a senior staff engineer asks: how would we leave this system? If the answer is 'we could not', the design has a hidden cost that nobody has priced. Lock-in is not always wrong, but it should be a conscious, costed decision rather than an accident. The question forces the team to think about abstraction layers, data formats, change streams and record versioning while those choices are still cheap.
deeper:
The question works because it reframes lock-in as a cost line rather than an abstract worry. If leaving would take a year of engineering, a full data rewrite, or downtime, that cost will eventually be paid, since the chapter's own rule is that every system is migrated within 5 to 10 years.

It also connects to other parts of the chapter. The design-doc checklist's Migration plan section explicitly includes 'how we would leave this system later', and the senior staff lens on design docs notes that deletion and migration are the two sections most often missing, both easy on day one and very hard to add in year three. Design-review question 24 asks: 'How would we migrate off this system in 5 years?' And the guidance on presenting a storage decision recommends showing the exit, because explaining how data would be moved out if the choice turns out wrong lowers the stakes of the decision and speeds approval.

quiz.q: Why does asking 'how would we leave this system?' help a design review?
quiz.a: It exposes lock-in as an unpriced cost; if leaving is impossible, the team must either justify that cost or add abstraction, CDC, open formats and versioning now.

section: Part 2: Choosing storage for a new system
title: Choose storage by data shape and access, not by product name
body: Start with the shape of the data and its access pattern, not with a product name. The chapter's flowchart is a first cut, not a rule. First question: is it large immutable blobs over 1 MB? If yes, use an object store such as S3, GCS, Azure Blob, Ambry or a Tectonic blob tenant. If not: is it append-only events or logs? If yes, use a log, Kafka for streaming, then lake tables for long-term analysis.
deeper:
Every arrow in the flowchart hides a trade-off covered in Chapters 2 to 7, so the chart is a way to start a conversation, not end it.

The first branch separates blobs because they behave differently from records: large, immutable objects suit erasure coding, CDN caching and cheap flat storage, and they bloat any database that holds them (a later anti-pattern). The 1 MB threshold is the chart's heuristic for 'large'.

The second branch catches append-only data such as logs and events. These are written sequentially, rarely updated, and read in bulk. A log like Kafka provides durable, ordered-per-partition ingestion for streaming consumers, and the data later lands in lake tables on object storage for analysis. Interview problem 9 builds exactly this pipeline.

The key takeaway puts the principle simply: start from data shape and access pattern, not product names, and expect the same app to need several stores.

quiz.q: According to the chapter's flowchart, what should large immutable blobs over 1 MB use, and why start with this question?
quiz.a: An object store (S3, GCS, Blob, Ambry, Tectonic). Blobs behave differently from records: immutable, large, suited to erasure coding and CDNs, and they bloat databases.

section: Part 2: Choosing storage for a new system
title: Scans go columnar; transactions go relational or distributed SQL
body: If data is not blobs or append-only logs, the flowchart asks: is it mostly scans and aggregates? If yes, use a columnar lake or warehouse such as Iceberg, BigQuery or Redshift. If not, ask whether you need multi-row transactions or joins. If yes and the data fits one primary region and under a few terabytes, use a relational database such as Postgres, MySQL or Aurora. If it is bigger or multi-region, use distributed SQL such as Spanner, CockroachDB or TiDB.
deeper:
Columnar storage stores each column together, which makes scans and aggregates over a few columns cheap and compresses well. That is why analytics goes to lakes and warehouses rather than row stores.

For transactional data, the chart's split is about scale and geography. A single-region relational database is the simplest, most mature option and handles a few terabytes comfortably, so it should be the default when it fits. Distributed SQL systems shard data across nodes and replicate with consensus, giving transactions and joins at larger scale or across regions, at the cost of more operational complexity and, for cross-region writes, higher latency.

The 'few TB' boundary is a heuristic, not a hard limit. The real question is whether one primary node and its replicas can carry the write load and data size for the planning horizon, which the modifiers table (size in 3 years) helps answer.

quiz.q: When does the flowchart send transactional data to distributed SQL instead of Postgres or MySQL?
quiz.a: When multi-row transactions or joins are needed but the data does not fit one primary region and under a few terabytes.

section: Part 2: Choosing storage for a new system
title: Huge-QPS single-key reads go key-value; add a cache for reads
body: For data that needs no transactions or joins, the flowchart asks: do you need single-key reads under 10 ms at huge QPS? If yes, use a key-value or wide-column store such as DynamoDB, Cassandra or Bigtable. If not, a document store or the relational default is fine. Finally, if the workload is read-heavy and can tolerate staleness, add a cache such as Memcached, Redis or EVCache in front to absorb reads.
deeper:
Key-value and wide-column stores trade query flexibility for predictable latency at scale: access is by key, data is partitioned across many nodes, and each read touches one partition. That fits workloads like sessions, user state and feeds that are looked up by ID millions of times per second.

When scale is moderate, the chart's advice is conservative: use a document store or simply stay with the relational default. Reaching for a specialized store without need adds operational cost.

The cache step is conditional on two properties. Read-heavy means a cache hit saves meaningful load. Tolerating staleness matters because caches can serve old values after a write; if readers must always see the latest data, caching needs careful invalidation, or write-through, which the trade-off catalog discusses. Interview problem 7 shows the full pattern for a profile service: a look-aside cache invalidated by CDC from the database, with leases to stop thundering herds.

quiz.q: What two conditions does the flowchart require before adding a cache like Memcached or Redis?
quiz.a: The workload must be read-heavy, so hits save real load, and able to tolerate staleness, since caches may briefly serve old values.

section: Part 2: Choosing storage for a new system
title: Modifiers: p99 latency and consistency reshape the first cut
body: After the flowchart's first cut, check modifiers. Latency: what is the p99 target? Under 1 ms means memory or local flash; under 10 ms means SSD-backed key-value storage; 100 ms and up allows object storage. Consistency: can a reader see stale data? If not, you need a single leader or consensus per key, and cross-region writes get slower. These two questions can overturn the flowchart's initial answer.
deeper:
The latency ladder maps directly to media and architecture. Sub-millisecond p99 is only achievable when data sits in RAM or on local flash with no network hop to a remote storage service. Ten milliseconds allows a networked SSD-backed store. Object storage, reached over HTTP with higher first-byte latency, fits workloads that tolerate 100 ms or more.

Consistency is about who orders writes. If a reader must always see the latest committed write, each key needs one authority, either a single leader or a consensus group such as Paxos or Raft, that orders writes. Across regions, that authority must talk over long-distance links, so writes pay cross-region round trips. The trade-off catalog lists the use cases: strong consistency for money, identity, inventory and uniqueness; eventual consistency for feeds, counters, caches and analytics. Getting this question wrong in either direction is costly: unnecessary strong consistency buys latency, and missing it produces subtle correctness bugs.

quiz.q: If readers must never see stale data, what does the storage design need, and what does it cost across regions?
quiz.a: A single leader or consensus per key to order writes; cross-region writes become slower because they pay long-distance round trips.

section: Part 2: Choosing storage for a new system
title: Modifiers: size, retention and compliance
body: Three more modifiers shape a storage choice. Size: what are total bytes and object count in 3 years? Object count drives metadata design, while bytes drive cost and tiering. Retention: how long is data kept and who deletes it? Long retention needs tiering and archival; short retention favours TTL-based stores that expire data automatically. Compliance: is there personal data, and in which regions? That requires deletion by user ID, residency pinning and per-tenant encryption keys (Chapter 11).
deeper:
These modifiers stretch the decision across time. Sizing for 3 years rather than today prevents choosing a system that must be migrated within a year. Separating object count from bytes echoes the metadata mental model: a small dataset with billions of tiny items can break a system sized only by capacity.

Retention decides whether the store needs lifecycle machinery. Data kept for years must move to cheaper tiers or archival storage; data kept for days is best in a store with a time-to-live (TTL) so expiry is automatic and nobody has to write a cleanup job.

Compliance adds hard constraints. Deletion by user ID means every dataset must know which column holds the user ID. Residency pinning means data must stay in allowed regions, which constrains replication. Per-tenant keys enable revoking one customer's access or crypto-shredding. Interview problem 4 on GDPR deletion shows how expensive these are to retrofit.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter separate object count from total bytes when sizing a new storage system?
quiz.a: Object count drives metadata design, while bytes drive cost and tiering; billions of small objects can break metadata even if total bytes are modest.

section: Part 2: Choosing storage for a new system
title: Modifiers: overwrite vs append, and can the data be rebuilt?
body: Two final modifiers. Write pattern: does the workload overwrite or append? Heavy overwrites favour B-trees, which update pages in place. Heavy writes and appends favour LSM trees, which buffer writes in memory and flush sorted files (Chapter 5). Rebuildable: can the data be recomputed from other data? Derived data can accept lower durability and use bulk-load paths, as LinkedIn's Venice does. Knowing data is derived can cut its cost dramatically.
deeper:
B-trees keep a balanced index and modify pages where they live, giving fast point reads and range scans and good behaviour for in-place updates. LSM trees convert random writes into sequential ones and compress well, which suits write-heavy workloads and flash, but they pay with background compaction.

The rebuildable question is often overlooked. Primary data, such as a user's uploaded photo, is irreplaceable and needs full durability and backups. Derived data, such as a search index, recommendation features or aggregated tables, can be regenerated from the primary source. So it may use fewer replicas, skip backups, and be refreshed by bulk-loading whole datasets rather than row-by-row writes. LinkedIn's Venice, open-sourced in 2022, is a derived-data platform built around that bulk-load path.

Design-review question 5 asks the same thing: 'Is this data primary or derived? Can it be rebuilt?' The answer can halve cost or double it.

quiz.q: Why can derived data use lower durability than primary data?
quiz.a: It can be recomputed from its source data, so losing it costs recomputation time rather than permanent loss; it can also use bulk-load paths like LinkedIn Venice.

section: Part 3: Reference architectures for the running example
title: One app, many stores: the 1-billion-user reference architecture
body: The running example is a global app with 1 billion users storing profiles, photos and videos, messages, logs and events, and analytics and ML data. Clients call API services backed by a Memcached or Redis cache. An upload service writes photos and videos to an erasure-coded object store served through CDN edge caches. Profiles live in sharded or distributed SQL; messages in a wide-column or LSM key-value store partitioned by conversation. Change data capture feeds Kafka, then a Parquet and Iceberg lake, then an archive tier.
deeper:
The diagram's lesson is that no single product serves every data type. Each store is chosen for its shape: small transactional records in SQL, large immutable media in object storage, write-heavy time-ordered messages in LSM-based stores, and bulk analytical data in columnar lake tables.

The connective tissue matters as much as the stores. Change data capture streams every database change into Kafka, which decouples the online stores from analytics: the lake is filled from events rather than by querying production databases. Lake data is stored as Parquet files organized into Iceberg tables on object storage, which keeps it in open formats readable by many engines. After the retention window, data moves to an archive tier rather than living on expensive storage forever.

The CDN in front of the object store absorbs hot reads near users, so the origin serves mostly cache misses and older content. This layered design is the template the chapter's interview answers reuse.

quiz.q: In the reference architecture, what role does change data capture play between online stores and the lake?
quiz.a: It streams every database change into Kafka, which feeds the Parquet/Iceberg lake, so analytics is filled from events instead of querying production databases.

section: Part 3: Reference architectures for the running example
title: Profiles: small, read-heavy records in SQL behind caches
body: Profiles are small records, read-heavy, with some transactions. They need secondary indexes and updates, and caches absorb the reads. The chapter maps implementations: Google uses Spanner; AWS uses Aurora or DynamoDB; Meta uses MySQL with MyRocks behind TAO and Memcache; open-source options are Postgres or MySQL with Vitess, CockroachDB or TiDB. The common pattern is a transactional store for correctness plus a cache layer to handle the read volume.
deeper:
Why SQL-style stores for profiles? Users look profiles up by many fields, such as username or email, which requires secondary indexes that stay consistent with the data. Updates, such as changing a username while keeping it unique, benefit from transactions.

Why caches? Profiles are read far more often than written; every page view, message and comment may display profile data. A cache layer like Meta's TAO and Memcache in front of MySQL absorbs that load so the database handles mostly writes and misses.

The options differ in how they scale. Aurora and Postgres are single-primary relational databases; Vitess shards MySQL horizontally; Spanner, CockroachDB and TiDB are distributed SQL with transactions across shards. DynamoDB is listed as an AWS alternative when access is mostly by key. Meta's use of MyRocks, MySQL with an LSM-based RocksDB engine, reflects the storage-efficiency migration described in Chapter 13. Interview problem 7 details the cache design for such a profile service.

quiz.q: Why does the reference architecture put profiles in a transactional SQL-style store rather than a pure key-value store?
quiz.a: Profiles need secondary indexes and transactional updates (such as unique usernames); caches in front absorb the heavy read traffic.

section: Part 3: Reference architectures for the running example
title: Photos and videos: immutable blobs, erasure-coded, tiered by age
body: Photos and videos are large immutable blobs, hot at first and then cold. Because they never change, erasure coding and CDN caching work well, and they can be tiered by age. Google stores them in Colossus via GCS; AWS uses S3 plus CloudFront; Meta uses a Tectonic blob tenant, formerly Haystack and f4; open-source choices are Ceph RGW and MinIO. Immutability is the property that makes this whole design cheap and simple.
deeper:
Immutability removes the hardest problems. With no in-place updates, there is no need to coordinate overwrites across erasure-coded fragments, and CDN caches never hold a stale version of the same object, only possibly-stale metadata such as privacy settings.

The hot-then-cold pattern drives tiering. Meta's history shows the evolution: Haystack handled hot photos by packing many into large files to cut metadata cost; f4 added a warm tier with cheaper erasure coding once read rates fell; later both were folded into Tectonic as a blob tenant.

The CDN layer, CloudFront in the AWS column, serves popular content from edge caches near users, so the object store's job becomes durability and serving the long tail. The capacity sketch in this part shows why this matters: roughly 128 PB per year of raw storage for photos alone, where the tiering policy matters more than which object store you pick.

quiz.q: Why do erasure coding and CDN caching work especially well for photos and videos?
quiz.a: The blobs are immutable: no in-place updates to coordinate across fragments, and cached copies never become stale versions of the object.

section: Part 3: Reference architectures for the running example
title: Messages: partition by conversation, cluster by time, use LSM
body: Messages are write-heavy, read by conversation, and time-ordered. The design partitions data by conversation ID and clusters it by time, so one conversation's messages sit together in order. LSM engines suit the heavy write load. Google uses Bigtable or Spanner; AWS uses DynamoDB; Meta uses MySQL with MyRocks and other internal stores; open-source options are Cassandra and ScyllaDB. The partition and clustering keys are the core of the design.
deeper:
The access pattern dictates the keys. Users almost always read one conversation at a time, recent messages first. Partitioning by conversation ID sends every read to one partition; clustering by time or sequence number makes 'last 50 messages' a single sequential range scan rather than scattered lookups.

Write-heavy workloads favour LSM trees, which buffer writes in memory and flush sorted files, converting random writes into sequential I/O. Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable and MyRocks are all LSM-based, which is why they appear in this row.

Interview problem 8 extends the design: append to an LSM-based store, replicate within the region using quorum writes, generate per-conversation sequence numbers from a single leader to guarantee ordering, cache recent messages, and tier old messages to cheaper storage. With end-to-end encryption the server stores only ciphertext, so search must happen on the device.

quiz.q: Why partition chat messages by conversation ID and cluster by time?
quiz.a: Reads target one conversation's recent messages; partitioning keeps them on one partition, and time clustering makes fetching the latest messages a single ordered range scan.

section: Part 3: Reference architectures for the running example
title: Logs and analytics: sequential writes, cheap objects, columnar scans
body: Logs and events are append-only, huge, and read in bulk. They suit sequential writes, cheap object storage and columnar formats for scans. Google uses Colossus files and BigQuery; AWS uses Kinesis or MSK into S3; Meta uses Scribe into the Tectonic warehouse; open source uses Kafka into Iceberg on object storage. Analytics and ML data is columnar, scan-heavy and in large files: BigQuery and Capacitor on Colossus, S3 with Athena, Redshift or S3 Tables, Tectonic with Presto and Spark, or Iceberg or Delta with Trino and Spark.
deeper:
The two rows share a principle: separate compute from storage. Data sits in cheap, durable object storage, and query engines are scaled independently on top. Open table formats such as Iceberg and Delta let many engines, including Trino, Spark and Presto, read the same tables, which avoids lock-in to one query system and eases future migrations.

For logs, the ingestion path is a durable log service first (Kafka, Kinesis, MSK or Meta's Scribe), then periodic batch writes into files in the warehouse or lake. This absorbs bursty producers and gives consumers ordered streams.

Columnar formats matter because analytical queries read a few columns across billions of rows. Storing each column together, as Capacitor at Google and Parquet in open source do, means reading only needed columns and compressing similar values together. Interview problem 9 spells out the pipeline: Parquet files every few minutes, committed as Iceberg snapshots, with compaction of small files and partitioning by date and event type.

quiz.q: Why do the analytics architectures separate compute from storage and use open table formats?
quiz.a: Cheap object storage holds data durably while engines scale independently; open formats like Iceberg or Delta let many engines read the same tables and ease migration.

section: Part 3: Reference architectures for the running example
title: Common mistake: one database for everything
body: Putting every data type in one database is simple on day one. By year three, logs are crowding out profile queries, photos are bloating backups, and every migration touches everything. The chapter's advice is to split storage by data type early, even if each store is small. Separate stores let each workload scale, fail and migrate on its own, instead of coupling unrelated data into one fragile system.
deeper:
The failure modes compound. Different data types have opposite access patterns: logs are write-heavy and scanned in bulk, profiles need low-latency point reads, and photos are large blobs. In one database, a log ingestion spike competes for the same disks, buffer cache and locks as user-facing profile queries, and tail latency suffers.

Blobs in the database inflate every backup, replica and snapshot, since every copy of a row carries the blob; the anti-pattern list calls this out separately. And migration becomes all-or-nothing: you cannot move logs to a lake without touching the database that also serves profiles.

Splitting early is cheap because each store starts small; splitting later requires the kind of zero-downtime migration the chapter's 50 PB problem describes. This mistake is a concrete example of the takeaway that the same app needs several stores.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter advise splitting storage by data type early, even when each store would be small?
quiz.a: One shared database lets workloads interfere (logs slowing profiles, blobs bloating backups) and couples all migrations; splitting is cheap early and very costly later.

section: Part 3: Reference architectures for the running example
title: Capacity sketch: photos for 1B users is about 128 PB a year
body: The chapter sketches photo capacity with labelled assumptions. Assume 10 percent of 1 billion users upload one photo per day, averaging 2 MB, plus 25 percent extra for resized versions. That is 100 million times 2.5 MB, or 250 TB per day logical. With RS(10,4) erasure coding at 1.4x, that becomes about 350 TB per day raw, roughly 128 PB per year. At this growth, the tiering policy matters more than the choice of object store.
deeper:
The method matters more than the exact numbers. Every input is an explicit assumption (upload rate, average size, resize overhead, redundancy scheme), so a reviewer who disagrees can change one input and recompute rather than argue about the conclusion. The chapter later says reviewers trust a wrong estimate with clear assumptions more than a vague claim.

The arithmetic: 1 billion times 10 percent is 100 million uploads per day. Two megabytes plus 25 percent gives 2.5 MB each. 100 million times 2.5 MB is 250 TB. Multiply by 1.4 for RS(10,4) to get 350 TB raw per day, and by 365 to get about 128 PB per year.

The conclusion is a senior staff insight: with that growth, moving cold photos to cheaper tiers, or re-encoding them with wider codes, saves far more than shaving a few percent off the object store's price. With 3x replication instead, raw growth would be over twice as large, which shows why erasure coding matters at this scale.

quiz.q: In the photo capacity sketch, why does the chapter conclude tiering policy matters more than the choice of object store?
quiz.a: At roughly 128 PB of raw growth per year, moving data to cheaper tiers as it cools dominates cost, dwarfing small price differences between object stores.

section: Part 4: How to write a storage design doc
title: Storage design docs differ: bytes outlive code
body: A storage design doc differs from a service design doc because bytes outlive code and mistakes stay on disk for years. The chapter gives a 16-part checklist. It opens with: context and goals, stating a single primary goal such as 'predictable p99 latency', as DynamoDB did; non-goals, such as no cross-region transactions; the data model, with entities, keys, sizes and a schema evolution plan; and access patterns, listing each query with QPS, read/write ratio, latency target and consistency need.
deeper:
A single primary goal forces prioritization. DynamoDB's design, described in its 2022 paper, centred on predictable latency, and that one goal guided countless smaller decisions. A doc with five equal goals gives reviewers no way to resolve conflicts between them.

Non-goals are just as important. Saying 'we will not support cross-region transactions' prevents scope creep and tells future users what not to expect, so they choose a different store if they need it.

The data model section needs a schema evolution plan because the schema will change and old records remain on disk. Design-review question 4 asks how the schema will change without downtime.

The access patterns section is where most storage choices are really made. Each query needs its rate, its read/write mix, its latency target and its consistency requirement, because these determine partitioning keys, indexes, caching and the engine. Listing them explicitly also reveals hot keys and queries that need secondary indexes early.

quiz.q: Why should a storage design doc state a single primary goal, such as DynamoDB's 'predictable p99 latency'?
quiz.a: A single goal gives a clear rule for resolving trade-offs; many equal goals leave reviewers and implementers no way to decide conflicts.

section: Part 4: How to write a storage design doc
title: Design doc core: capacity, durability math, availability, failures
body: The middle of the checklist covers the numbers and failures. Capacity plan: bytes and object counts today, in 1 year and 3 years, growth assumptions, and a headroom target, for example staying under 70 percent as Azure stamps do. Durability math: replication or erasure code, failure domains, repair time, estimated annual loss probability, plus backups and their restore time. Availability and consistency: the SLO, region layout, and behaviour during a network partition. Failure modes: each with detection, impact and recovery.
deeper:
These sections turn claims into checkable numbers. A capacity plan with both bytes and object counts catches metadata limits early. The headroom target defines when to add capacity, and the related review question asks who gets paged when it is crossed.

Durability math applies the repair-speed model: given the redundancy scheme, the failure domains copies are spread across, and the repair time, estimate how likely data loss is per year. It also demands backup restore times, since a backup that takes a week to restore may not meet recovery needs.

The availability section must say what happens during a partition: which side keeps accepting writes, and what readers see.

The failure-mode list is deliberately broad: disk, node, rack, zone and region loss; a hot key; a bad deploy; a corrupt write; and operator error. For each, the doc states how it is detected, what the impact is, and how the system recovers. Operator error and corrupt writes are included because replication faithfully copies mistakes too.

quiz.q: Why does the design-doc checklist list operator error and corrupt writes as failure modes alongside hardware loss?
quiz.a: Replication and redundancy protect against hardware failures but faithfully copy bad writes and mistakes, so these need their own detection and recovery plans.

section: Part 4: How to write a storage design doc
title: Design doc: security, compliance, lifecycle and operations
body: The next four checklist sections cover obligations that outlast launch. Security: encryption at rest and in transit, key management, access control and audit logs. Compliance review: a personal data inventory, residency, retention, a deletion path by user ID, and legal hold. Lifecycle: temperature over time, tiering rules, TTLs, archival and deletion. Operations: upgrades, schema changes, resharding, on-call runbooks and dashboards. Each is cheap to design up front and expensive to retrofit.
deeper:
Security and compliance are separate sections because they answer different questions. Security asks who can read the data and how it is protected; compliance asks what laws require about where it lives, how long it stays, and how it is removed. A deletion path by user ID is only possible if every dataset records which column holds the user ID, which is the data inventory step in interview problem 4. Legal hold is the opposite requirement: a block on deletion for legal reasons, which the deletion machinery must respect.

The lifecycle section operationalizes the temperature mental model: it states when data becomes warm or cold, which tier it moves to, when TTLs expire it, and who deletes it.

The operations section acknowledges that storage systems run for years. Engine upgrades, schema changes and resharding will happen; runbooks and dashboards must exist before the first incident. Design-review questions on upgrades without downtime and on rolling back versions that already wrote new formats test this section.

quiz.q: Why does a deletion path by user ID need to be designed in the compliance section rather than added later?
quiz.a: It requires every dataset to record which column holds the user ID; retrofitting that across stores, caches, lakes and backups is very hard.

section: Part 4: How to write a storage design doc
title: Design doc: migration, cost model, alternatives, open risks
body: The checklist ends with four sections. Migration plan: how data gets in through backfill, dual-write or CDC, verification, cutover and rollback, and also how you would leave this system later. Cost model: storage, requests, network egress, replication, backup and people, expressed as cost per user or per GB-month. Alternatives considered: at least two, with why they lost. Open questions and risks: what is still unknown. Together these make the decision reviewable and reversible.
deeper:
The migration section covers both directions: getting data in, since a new system usually starts by importing from an old one, and getting data out later. The entry path uses the same toolkit as the 50 PB migration problem: backfill history, dual-write or stream changes via CDC, verify with checksums and counts, cut over gradually, and keep a rollback path.

The cost model is broader than storage price. Requests, egress (data leaving a cloud or region, often billed), extra replicas, backups and the people who operate the system can each exceed raw capacity cost. Normalizing to cost per user or per GB-month makes growth scenarios comparable.

Requiring at least two real alternatives shows the chosen design won a comparison rather than being assumed. Listing open questions and risks is a sign of maturity: reviewers can focus on real uncertainty instead of hunting for hidden gaps.

quiz.q: Why should a storage cost model include egress, replication, backups and people, not just storage price?
quiz.a: Each of these can rival or exceed raw capacity cost; ignoring them makes a design look cheaper than it will be to run.

section: Part 4: How to write a storage design doc
title: Senior staff lens: deletion and migration are the missing sections
body: The two design-doc sections most often missing are deletion and migration. Both are easy to design on day one and very hard to add in year three. On day one, adding a user-ID column, a per-user key, a TTL, a CDC stream or an abstraction layer is a small change. In year three, with petabytes on disk and dozens of dependent teams, the same capability requires scanning, rewriting and migrating everything. The key takeaway says: write them first.
deeper:
Why do teams skip them? Neither affects launch. The system works fine without a deletion path until a GDPR request or cost review arrives, and works fine without a migration plan until the system must be replaced, which the chapter says happens within 5 to 10 years.

The cost asymmetry is dramatic. Deletion retrofitted means discovering where personal data lives across databases, caches, object stores, search indexes, logs, the lake, ML training sets and backups, then building fan-out deletion for each. Interview problem 4 shows how many moving parts that takes even when designed deliberately. Migration retrofitted means building routing layers, dual writes and reconciliation logic around a system that was never designed for it, and often discovering records lack versions or timestamps needed to reconcile.

Writing these sections first flips the incentives: they shape the data model rather than fighting it.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter recommend writing the deletion and migration sections of a design doc first?
quiz.a: They are the most often missing, yet cheap to build into the data model on day one and extremely costly to retrofit once data and dependents accumulate.

title: Review questions: data model and access
body: The chapter lists 36 design-review questions in seven groups. The data model and access group asks: What is the largest single item, and what happens if it is 100x larger? What is the hottest key and its peak QPS? Which queries need a secondary index, and is that index transactional with the data? How will the schema change without downtime? Is this data primary or derived, and can it be rebuilt? These expose the extremes a design must survive.
deeper:
Each question targets a known failure pattern. The 100x-larger item probes limits: a design that assumes 10 KB rows may break when one user stores a 1 MB document, hitting row-size limits, blowing up caches or making replication lag.

The hottest key question catches skew. Averages hide the celebrity account or viral object that receives far more traffic than others and saturates one shard.

The transactional-index question comes from real pain. If the application writes data and index separately without atomicity, a crash between the writes leaves them inconsistent forever; Pinterest named this a key reason for moving its graph store to TiDB.

Schema changes without downtime matter because records written in old schemas stay on disk. And the primary-versus-derived question decides how much durability and backup the data truly needs, since derived data can be rebuilt from its sources.

quiz.q: Why is 'Is the secondary index transactional with the data?' an important review question?
quiz.a: If data and index are written separately without atomicity, a crash between writes leaves them permanently inconsistent, as Pinterest experienced before moving to TiDB.

title: Review questions: capacity and scaling
body: The capacity and scaling group asks: What are the object count and byte count in 3 years? What is the resharding plan, and has it been tested? Which resource runs out first: IOPS, capacity, CPU, memory, or metadata? What is the headroom target, and who gets paged when it is crossed? Does anything scale with the number of files rather than bytes? These questions force a team to find its first bottleneck before production does.
deeper:
Counting both objects and bytes for 3 years applies the metadata mental model: object count drives metadata design, bytes drive cost.

Resharding, changing how data is split into shards, is often designed but never exercised. An untested resharding plan tends to fail exactly when it is needed, under peak load with hot shards, so the question asks whether it has actually been run.

'Which resource runs out first' pushes past capacity planning by bytes. A workload might have ample disk but exhaust IOPS, CPU for compaction, memory for indexes, or metadata operations first, and each implies a different mitigation.

The headroom question has two halves: a number and an owner. A target without paging means capacity silently runs out.

The final question hunts for hidden O(number of files) behaviour, such as listing, scanning or rebuilding that grows with file count. Small-file workloads trigger it even when total bytes look modest.

quiz.q: Why does the review ask whether the resharding plan has been tested, not just whether it exists?
quiz.a: Untested resharding tends to fail when it is finally needed, under peak load with hot shards; only a real exercise proves it works.

title: Review questions: durability and reliability
body: The durability and reliability group asks: What is the repair time after a disk or node loss? How many failures can one item survive, and are copies in independent failure domains? How do we detect silent corruption, and are checksums end-to-end? When did we last restore from backup, and how long did it take? Can an operator or a bug delete everything, and what stops it? What is the blast radius of one bad deploy?
deeper:
Repair time comes first because the chapter's durability model says it matters more than copy count.

The failure-domain question guards against correlated failures. Three copies on one rack are one rack failure away from loss; copies must sit in independent failure domains such as racks, zones or regions.

Silent corruption, data that changes without an error, is caught only by checksums verified along the whole path from writer to reader and by background scrubbing. Checksums checked only at the disk miss corruption introduced in memory or on the network.

The backup question asks for a date and a duration, because a backup that has never been restored is, in the chapter's words, a hope, not a backup.

Mass deletion by operator or bug is a real risk that replication cannot fix, since deletes replicate too. Defenses named are soft delete, delayed purge and object lock, which prevents deletion for a period. Blast radius of a bad deploy tests whether cells or stamps actually contain failures.

quiz.q: Why doesn't replication protect against an operator or bug deleting everything, and what does?
quiz.a: Deletes replicate to every copy. Protection comes from soft delete, delayed purge, and object lock (WORM protection that prevents deletion for a period).

title: Review questions: consistency and correctness
body: The consistency and correctness group asks: What does a reader see during a failover? How are concurrent writes to the same key resolved? What happens to in-flight writes if a region is lost, and what is the RPO, the recovery point objective or how much data you may lose? Are cache invalidations reliable, or can the cache stay stale forever? These questions surface the subtle bugs that appear only under failure or concurrency.
deeper:
Failover is when consistency promises are most likely to break. During a leader change, a reader may see stale data from a lagging replica, or writes acknowledged by the old leader may be missing on the new one. The design must state what users observe.

Concurrent writes need a defined resolution rule. Options covered in the chapter include a single leader per key that orders writes, last-writer-wins timestamps that can silently drop updates, and CRDTs that merge without coordination.

Region loss plus asynchronous replication means recent writes may be lost. The RPO makes that loss explicit and agreed; if it must be zero, cross-region replication must be synchronous, with a latency cost.

The cache question targets a specific failure: an invalidation message lost once leaves a cache entry stale indefinitely. Interview problem 7 answers it by invalidating via CDC from the database, not only from application code, and alerting on stale-read rate rather than only latency.

quiz.q: Why might a cache 'stay stale forever', and how does the chapter suggest preventing it?
quiz.a: If an invalidation is missed (for example a writer forgets or a message is lost), nothing refreshes the entry. Invalidate via CDC from the database and alert on stale-read rate.

title: Review questions: operations, change and security
body: Operations questions: How do we upgrade the storage engine without downtime? How do we roll back a bad version that already wrote data in a new format? Are the top three alerts actionable? How would we migrate off this system in 5 years? Security questions: Where is personal data, and can we find it all by user ID? How long after a deletion request is data gone everywhere? Which regions may it live in, and what enforces it? Who holds encryption keys, and can one tenant's key be revoked? Are access logs kept and reviewed?
deeper:
The rollback question is uniquely a storage problem. Rolling back code is easy, but if the new version already wrote records in a new format, the old version may not read them. Safe designs make readers understand new formats before writers produce them.

The alert question asks for top three and actionable, because noisy alerts train on-call engineers to ignore them.

The deletion question lists every place data hides: primary stores, caches, replicas, backups and the lake. A deletion that clears the primary database but leaves copies in the lake or backups is incomplete. Crypto-shredding handles backups by deleting a per-user key.

The residency question asks not only which regions are allowed but what enforces it, since a policy without a technical control will eventually be violated by a replication change.

Per-tenant key revocation depends on customer-managed or per-tenant keys, which the trade-off catalog notes enable per-tenant revocation and crypto-shredding.

quiz.q: Why is rolling back a storage engine version harder than rolling back ordinary service code?
quiz.a: The new version may already have written data in a new format that the old version cannot read, so the rollback breaks unless formats were made compatible.

title: Review questions: cost and organization
body: Cost questions: What is the cost per GB-month and per million requests, including replicas and backups? What share of stored data has not been read in 90 days? What is the egress cost of the main read path? What does the default retention cost in 3 years? Organization questions: Which team owns this data, and who approves schema changes? How many other teams will depend on it, and through what interface? What is the simplest version that could work, and why is it not enough?
deeper:
The cost questions push past the headline price. Replicas and backups multiply storage; request charges can dominate for small objects; and egress on the main read path can exceed storage cost for data served across regions or out of a cloud. The 90-day question measures how much data is cold and therefore a tiering opportunity. The default-retention question prices the policy of doing nothing.

The organization questions recognize that storage systems are shared infrastructure. Ownership must be explicit: who owns the data and who approves schema changes. Dependents matter because each team that reads the data directly, rather than through a stable interface, becomes a blocker for future migrations; the chapter's migration model relies on an abstraction layer.

The last question, 'what is the simplest version that could work, and why is it not enough?', is a guard against over-engineering. It forces a design to justify every piece of complexity against a simpler baseline.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of asking 'What share of stored data has not been read in 90 days?'
quiz.a: It measures how much data is cold, revealing tiering or deletion opportunities and whether data is being paid for without being used.

title: Replication vs erasure coding; B-tree vs LSM tree
body: The trade-off catalog pairs options with when to pick each. Redundancy: choose replication for hot, small, latency-sensitive data; choose erasure coding for warm or cold, large objects when cost matters. Storage engine: choose a B-tree for read-heavy workloads with in-place updates and range scans; choose an LSM tree for write-heavy workloads, compression and flash. Neither option in either pair is better in general; the workload decides.
deeper:
Replication keeps full copies, so any single copy serves a read directly and repair is a simple copy, which is why it suits hot, latency-sensitive data. Erasure coding stores data plus parity fragments, cutting overhead to about 1.4x for RS(10,4) versus 3x, but small reads may span nodes and repair reads many fragments. Many systems use both, replicating new hot data and re-encoding it as it cools, as Meta did moving from Haystack to f4.

B-trees update pages in place, keeping one current copy of each key, which gives predictable reads and efficient range scans. LSM trees buffer writes in memory and flush sorted immutable files, turning random writes into sequential ones and compressing well, which suits flash. The cost is background compaction and potential read amplification across multiple files. The Part 2 modifier table uses the same split: heavy overwrites favour B-trees; heavy writes and appends favour LSM trees.

quiz.q: When does the trade-off catalog recommend an LSM tree over a B-tree?
quiz.a: For write-heavy workloads, where compression matters, and on flash; B-trees are better for read-heavy workloads with in-place updates and range scans.

title: Strong vs eventual; single leader vs multi-leader; sync vs async
body: Consistency: choose strong for money, identity, inventory and uniqueness; eventual for feeds, counters, caches and analytics. Replication topology: a single leader gives simple reasoning and transactions; leaderless or multi-leader gives always-writable, multi-region writes. Cross-region replication: synchronous when RPO must be zero; asynchronous when latency matters more than the last few seconds of data. Each choice buys one property by paying with another.
deeper:
Strong consistency means every read sees the latest committed write; eventual consistency means replicas converge if writes stop, but reads may be stale. Money and uniqueness break under staleness, as with double-spending or two users with one username; a feed that is a second behind does not.

A single leader orders every write for a shard, making reasoning and transactions straightforward, but writes stop when the leader is unreachable. Leaderless and multi-leader designs, the Dynamo and Cassandra family, accept writes anywhere, at the cost of conflict resolution, where last-writer-wins can lose concurrent updates.

Synchronous cross-region replication waits for a remote acknowledgment, so a region loss loses nothing but every write pays a round trip. Asynchronous replication acknowledges locally and ships later, so a region loss can drop recent writes. The anti-pattern list warns against making synchronous cross-region writes the default rather than an explicit per-dataset choice backed by an RPO requirement.

quiz.q: When should cross-region replication be synchronous rather than asynchronous?
quiz.a: When the RPO must be zero, meaning no data loss on region failure is acceptable; otherwise asynchronous saves write latency at the risk of losing the last seconds.

title: Cells vs pools, central vs sharded metadata, coupled vs disaggregated
body: Failure domain: choose small cells or stamps when blast radius is the top risk; a giant shared pool when stranded capacity is the top cost. Metadata: a central master for small scale and simplicity; a sharded metadata store for billions of files. Storage and compute: coupled, meaning local disk, for lowest latency and predictable workloads; disaggregated, meaning network storage, for elastic compute and independent scaling. These are the architectural choices hardest to reverse later.
deeper:
The cells-versus-pool choice echoes Meta and Azure: Meta built large Tectonic clusters to use capacity efficiently, while Azure's fixed-size stamps bound failure. A shared pool then needs per-tenant quotas and priority classes to prevent one tenant from starving others.

Central versus sharded metadata follows the GFS and HDFS story: a single master is simple and fast until file counts outgrow its memory, after which Google and Meta moved metadata into sharded key-value stores (Bigtable and ZippyDB).

Disaggregation separates storage from compute so each scales alone. Coupled designs read from local disk with no network hop, giving the lowest latency and predictable performance, but compute and storage must grow together, and a failed machine takes its data with it. Disaggregated designs let compute scale elastically, as in the lake and warehouse architectures where many query engines sit on shared object storage, at the cost of network latency and bandwidth.

quiz.q: What does disaggregating storage from compute buy, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: Elastic compute and independent scaling of storage and compute, at the cost of network latency and bandwidth compared with coupled local disks.

title: Look-aside vs write-through, soft vs hard delete, auto vs manual tiers
body: Cache: look-aside suits read-heavy data that tolerates staleness; write-through suits cases where the cache must stay fresh on write. Deletion: hard delete now when compliance deadlines are tight; soft delete with a later purge to protect against mistakes and bugs. Tiering: automatic by access when patterns are unknown; explicit by policy when lifecycles are predictable or legal rules apply. Each pair trades simplicity or safety against freshness or control.
deeper:
In a look-aside cache, the application checks the cache, and on a miss reads the database and fills the cache; writes go to the database and invalidate the cache. It is simple, but a missed invalidation leaves stale data. Write-through updates the cache as part of each write, keeping it fresh at the cost of extra write latency and coupling.

Hard versus soft delete is a tension between two risks. Soft delete, marking data deleted and purging later, lets you recover from an operator mistake or a buggy mass delete, one of the durability review questions. But compliance deadlines may require data to be truly gone quickly, so the purge delay must fit inside the legal window. The photo-storage interview answer combines both: soft delete immediately in metadata, physical delete by compaction within the compliance window.

Automatic tiering, such as S3 Intelligent-Tiering, adapts per object when you cannot predict access; explicit lifecycle rules are better when you know the lifecycle or must follow legal rules.

quiz.q: When is soft delete with a delayed purge preferable to immediate hard delete?
quiz.a: When protecting against operator mistakes and bugs matters more; hard delete wins when compliance deadlines are tight. The purge delay must fit inside any legal window.

title: Build vs buy, proprietary vs open formats, whose encryption keys
body: Build versus buy: build when storage is your product or your top cost; use a managed service when storage is not your differentiator. Format: proprietary for deep optimization for one engine; open formats such as Parquet and Iceberg when many engines or future migrations matter. Encryption keys: provider-managed for simplicity; customer-managed for per-tenant revocation and crypto-shredding. These choices decide how much control you keep and how much work you take on.
deeper:
Build versus buy follows the economics seen in Chapter 13. Dropbox left S3 to build Magic Pocket because storage was both central to its product and its dominant cost, so the engineering investment paid back. For most companies, storage is plumbing, and a managed service's operational burden savings outweigh a possibly higher unit price.

The format choice ties to the migration mental model. A proprietary format can be tuned tightly to one engine, but data that must live for years in a format only one engine reads turns every future migration into a full rewrite. Open formats let Trino, Spark and other engines read the same tables.

Key ownership is about control. Provider-managed keys are simplest. Customer-managed or per-tenant keys let you revoke a single tenant's access and enable crypto-shredding, deleting data by destroying its key, which the GDPR interview problem uses to make backups unreadable for a deleted user without rewriting them. The cost is key-management load.

quiz.q: When does the trade-off catalog say a company should build its own storage rather than buy a managed service?
quiz.a: When storage is its product or its top cost, as with Dropbox's Magic Pocket; otherwise a managed service is better because storage is not a differentiator.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
title: Anti-pattern: using the database as a queue
body: The database-as-queue anti-pattern is a table with a 'status' column that many workers poll for new jobs. It works at small scale. At large scale, the polling queries and row locks fight with user traffic on the same database. The fix is to use a log such as Kafka or a real queue for work distribution, and keep the database for state. Like the other anti-patterns, it looks fine in review and fails in year two or three.
deeper:
Why does it degrade? Every worker repeatedly runs a query like 'find rows where status is pending', then locks a row to claim it. As workers multiply, polling load grows even when there is no work, and workers contend for the same rows, creating lock contention. Because the table lives in the primary database, this contention slows user-facing queries that share the same resources.

Logs and queues are built for this: consumers read sequentially from partitions or receive pushed messages, without scanning tables or taking row locks. The database then holds only durable state, such as the job's result.

The chapter's senior staff lens uses this anti-pattern as its example of how to push back effectively: not just 'no', but a dated, numbered prediction such as 'This polling table will hit lock contention at about 5,000 workers, which is our plan for Q3.' The chapter notes each anti-pattern has appeared in some form in the migrations described in Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Why does a polling 'status' table stop working as a job queue at large scale?
quiz.a: Many workers' polling queries and row locks contend with each other and with user traffic on the same database, causing lock contention and slowdowns.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
title: Anti-pattern: storing blobs inside database rows
body: Storing images or large JSON documents inside database rows looks convenient but is an anti-pattern. Backups, replication and caches all slow down because every copy of the row carries the blob. The fix is to store the blob in an object store and keep only a pointer and a checksum in the database row. The database stays small and fast for the structured queries it is good at, while the object store handles large bytes cheaply.
deeper:
The cost is multiplied across every copy. A database typically has several replicas, regular backups, a replication log and often a cache in front. A 2 MB image inside a row is copied to all of these, so replication lag grows, backups take longer and cost more, and caches hold fewer useful rows. Row-oriented engines also read more bytes than needed when queries touch only small fields.

Object stores are designed for large immutable blobs: cheap per byte, erasure-coded, and CDN-friendly. The row keeps a pointer to the object, plus a checksum so the application can verify the blob it fetches is the one that was written, detecting corruption or mismatched pointers.
