This anti-pattern is also one reason the chapter's 'one database for everything' common mistake hurts: photos bloat backups. The flowchart in Part 2 routes blobs over 1 MB straight to an object store for the same reason.

quiz.q: Why should a database row store a pointer and checksum instead of the blob itself?
quiz.a: Every row copy (replicas, backups, caches) would carry the blob, slowing all of them; object stores hold large bytes cheaply, and the checksum verifies the fetched blob.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
title: Anti-pattern: unbounded partitions like 'country' or 'day'
body: An unbounded partition uses a partition key such as 'country' or 'day' that grows without limit. Eventually one partition becomes hot and too large to move: all of today's writes land on the 'day' partition, or one populous country holds a huge share of users. The fix is to pick a partition key with high cardinality, meaning many distinct values, or to add a bucket suffix that spreads one logical key across several physical partitions.
deeper:
Partitioning only spreads load if keys spread evenly. A low-cardinality key has few distinct values, so data piles up on a handful of partitions regardless of cluster size. A time-based key is worse for writes: every current write goes to the newest partition, creating a hot spot that moves daily.

Once a partition is too big, it cannot be rebalanced to another node without moving massive amounts of data, and it may exceed per-partition limits in the storage engine.

A bucket suffix works like this: instead of keying by 'day', key by 'day plus bucket number', where the bucket is derived from, say, a hash of the record ID modulo N. Writes spread across N partitions, and a reader wanting a whole day queries all N buckets. This trades slightly more complex reads for evenly spread writes. The design-review question about the hottest key and its peak QPS aims to catch this early.

quiz.q: How does adding a bucket suffix fix a hot 'day' partition?
quiz.a: It splits one logical key into N physical partitions (such as day plus hash modulo N), spreading writes evenly; readers query all N buckets to get the whole day.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
title: Anti-pattern: app-maintained indexes without transactions
body: An application-maintained index without transactions means two separate writes, one for the data and one for the index, with no atomicity. If the process crashes between them, the data and index are left inconsistent forever: records that cannot be found, or index entries pointing at nothing. Pinterest named this as a key reason for moving its graph store to TiDB, a distributed SQL database with transactional secondary indexes (Chapter 13).
deeper:
This pattern arises when a store offers fast key lookups but no secondary indexes, so applications build their own by writing an extra lookup row. It works most of the time, which is why it passes review. But crashes, timeouts and partial failures happen constantly at scale, and each one between the two writes leaves a permanent mismatch. Nothing detects or repairs it unless someone builds a reconciliation job.

The fix is to store data where the index is updated in the same transaction as the data, or to use a store that maintains secondary indexes itself. Design-review question 3 asks exactly this: which queries need a secondary index, and is that index transactional with the data?

Pinterest's move from HBase to TiDB, documented in a PingCAP case study, illustrates that the pain accumulates until a migration becomes the cheapest fix.

quiz.q: Why does an application-maintained index without transactions become inconsistent over time?
quiz.a: Data and index are two separate writes; any crash between them leaves one without the other, and nothing repairs the mismatch automatically.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
title: Anti-pattern: cache as the source of truth
body: The cache-as-source-of-truth anti-pattern is a service that writes only to the cache and promises to 'flush later' to durable storage. When the cache node dies, the unflushed data is lost. The chapter's rule is that caches must be rebuildable from a durable store. A cache is an optimization for reads; if losing it loses data, it is actually an unreliable database without the durability guarantees a real database provides.
deeper:
The pattern is tempting because cache writes are fast and cheap, and flushing in batches reduces load on the database. But cache systems like Memcached keep data in memory and are designed on the assumption that their contents can be discarded: nodes restart, evict entries under memory pressure, and fail without replicating their state durably.

The correct model is that the durable store is written first and the cache is derived from it. Then any cache node can be lost and refilled from the database, at the cost of a temporary drop in hit rate. The trade-off catalog's look-aside and write-through patterns both keep the database as the truth; they differ only in when the cache is updated.

This ties to the 'rebuildable' modifier in Part 2: caches are pure derived data, so they can have low durability precisely because the source of truth is elsewhere.

quiz.q: What rule prevents the 'cache as source of truth' anti-pattern?
quiz.a: Caches must be rebuildable from a durable store: write durable storage first, and treat the cache as derived data that can be lost and refilled.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
title: Anti-pattern: retention by nobody
body: Retention by nobody means a dataset has no TTL, no lifecycle rule and no owner. Nobody decided to keep it forever; nobody decided anything. The dataset grows until it becomes a cost incident, when the bill gets noticed, or a compliance incident, when personal data is kept long past any legitimate need. The fix is to assign an owner and a retention rule when the dataset is created, and to make a safe expiry the default.
deeper:
This is the operational form of two mental models. The lifecycle model asks 'who deletes it?' and warns that if nobody can answer, the data will be kept forever and paid for forever. The defaults model notes that whatever the platform does by default, most teams keep, so a default of infinite retention silently applies to most datasets.

The cost dimension compounds: storage grows each year, plus its replicas and backups. The compliance dimension compounds too: every extra year of personal data raises risk under laws like GDPR, and deletion requests must search ever larger stores.

Preventions from elsewhere in the chapter: a Lifecycle section in every design doc; a data inventory that declares ownership and personal data per dataset ('no declaration, no deploy'); TTL-based stores for short-lived data; and the review questions 'What does the default retention cost in 3 years?' and 'What share of stored data has not been read in 90 days?'

quiz.q: What two kinds of incidents does 'retention by nobody' eventually cause?
quiz.a: A cost incident, as the dataset grows without limit, or a compliance incident, as personal data is kept far longer than justified.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
title: Anti-pattern: cross-region synchronous writes by default
body: Making cross-region synchronous replication the default means every write pays a cross-region round trip, even for data that could tolerate a few seconds of loss. That inflates latency and cost across the whole platform for durability most datasets never needed. The fix is to make synchronous replication an explicit choice per dataset, backed by a stated RPO requirement, the recovery point objective describing how much data may be lost in a disaster.
deeper:
Synchronous cross-region replication waits for a remote region to acknowledge each write before confirming it. That guarantees no loss on region failure, an RPO of zero, but adds long-distance network latency to every write and doubles or more the replication cost. For money or uniqueness constraints, that price may be right. For logs, feeds, analytics or caches, losing a few seconds of recent writes in a rare region outage is acceptable, and asynchronous replication is much cheaper and faster.

This is a case of the wrong-default mental model: the chapter notes that if the default replication is cross-region, cost doubles for data that never needed it. Because teams rarely change defaults, a conservative-looking default quietly becomes an expensive policy.

The trade-off catalog states the rule: synchronous when RPO must be zero; asynchronous when latency matters more than the last seconds of data.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't cross-region synchronous replication be the platform default?
quiz.a: Every write would pay a cross-region round trip and extra cost even for data that tolerates a few seconds of loss; it should be chosen per dataset based on RPO.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
title: Anti-pattern: backups that were never restored
body: A backup that has never been restored in a drill is a hope, not a backup. Backups can silently fail: jobs skip files, formats change, encryption keys go missing, or restore takes far longer than anyone assumed. The Google SRE book's data-integrity chapter makes this point strongly: what matters is the restore, not the backup. The fix is regular restore drills that measure both success and duration.
deeper:
Backups are unusual infrastructure because their real test happens only in a disaster, which is the worst time to discover they do not work. Common silent failures include backing up the wrong dataset, missing tables added after the backup job was written, corrupted archives, dependencies on keys or tooling that no longer exist, and restores so slow they cannot meet the recovery time objective (RTO), meaning how long recovery may take.

Drills convert assumptions into evidence. Design-review question 14 asks precisely: 'When did we last restore from backup, and how long did it take?' A date and a duration are the only acceptable answers. The design-doc checklist similarly asks for backups and their restore time in the durability section.

Backups remain essential even with replication, because replication copies mistakes and deletes instantly, while backups preserve older points in time. The chapter's SRE reference is Chapter 26, 'Data Integrity: What You Read Is What You Wrote' (2016).

quiz.q: Why does the chapter call an untested backup 'a hope, not a backup'?
quiz.a: Backups can fail silently (missing data, lost keys, slow restores); only a restore drill proves the data can actually be recovered and how long it takes.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
title: Anti-pattern: one giant shared cluster with no quotas
body: A giant shared storage cluster with no quotas lets one tenant's batch job saturate the disks, and every online service slows down with it. Shared storage needs per-tenant quotas and priority classes, as Meta's Tectonic provides through its traffic classes (Chapter 2). Big shared pools are efficient, but only if the system can stop one noisy tenant from consuming everyone's I/O. Without isolation, pooling capacity also pools failure.
deeper:
This anti-pattern is the downside of the stranded-capacity trade-off. Meta deliberately chose large Tectonic clusters to use capacity efficiently rather than splitting it into many small units. That choice works because Tectonic isolates tenants: quotas cap how much each tenant can consume, and traffic classes prioritize latency-sensitive online requests over bulk background work.

Without those controls, contention is inevitable. Batch analytics, backfills, compactions and repair traffic are throughput-hungry and can issue enormous amounts of I/O. Online services need low tail latency and suffer the most when disks are saturated.

The alternative, from the blast radius model, is to use cells or stamps so a noisy tenant affects only its own slice. The trade-off catalog frames the choice: small cells when blast radius is the top risk, a giant pool when stranded capacity is the top cost. A giant pool with no quotas gets the risks of both and the safety of neither.

quiz.q: What makes a large shared storage cluster safe to use, according to the chapter?
quiz.a: Per-tenant quotas and priority classes, like Tectonic's traffic classes, so one tenant's batch job cannot saturate disks and slow every online service.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
title: Anti-pattern: proprietary formats for long-lived data
body: Storing data that must live for ten years in a format only one engine can read is an anti-pattern. When that engine is eventually replaced, which the chapter says happens to every storage system within 5 to 10 years, the next migration becomes a full rewrite of all the data. Open formats such as Parquet and Iceberg let multiple engines read the same data, so changing engines does not require rewriting the bytes.
deeper:
The problem is that a format ties data to software. If only one engine can decode files, then leaving that engine means reading every byte with the old engine and writing it again in something new. At petabyte scale that is a months-long, bandwidth-bound project, as the 50 PB migration estimate shows.

The trade-off catalog acknowledges why teams choose proprietary formats: deep optimization for one engine can yield better performance or compression. That can be right for short-lived or derived data. For long-lived primary data, flexibility usually matters more.

The chapter's day-one migration habits include keeping data in open formats where possible, and the analytics architectures in Part 3 all lean on open table formats (Iceberg, Delta) so many engines such as Trino, Spark and Presto can query the same tables. This anti-pattern is the mirror image of that advice.

quiz.q: Why are proprietary formats risky specifically for long-lived data?
quiz.a: Every storage engine is eventually replaced; if only one engine reads the format, leaving it means rewriting all the data, a huge migration.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
title: Senior staff lens: reject with a dated, numbered prediction
body: When you find an anti-pattern in a review, do not only say 'no'. Say what it will cost and when. For example: 'This polling table will hit lock contention at about 5,000 workers, which is our plan for Q3.' The chapter argues that a dated, numbered prediction changes minds faster than a principle. It turns an abstract best practice into a concrete, checkable risk tied to the team's own roadmap.
deeper:
Principles invite debate: a team can reasonably argue that 'databases make bad queues' does not apply to their small workload. A prediction grounded in their numbers is harder to dismiss and easier to verify. It connects the anti-pattern to something the team already cares about, their own growth plan, and gives a deadline.

It also shows respect for the design. Anti-patterns work at small scale, which is why they pass review; the prediction acknowledges that the design is fine today and pinpoints when it stops being fine. That makes it easier for the team to accept a change, or to consciously accept the risk with a plan to revisit before the threshold.

The same philosophy appears in the guidance on presenting storage decisions: show the numbers with assumptions labelled, because reviewers trust a wrong estimate with clear assumptions more than a vague claim, since they can fix the assumptions.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter suggest a dated, numbered prediction rather than citing a principle when rejecting an anti-pattern?
quiz.a: It ties the risk to the team's own numbers and roadmap, making it concrete and checkable; principles invite debate, predictions change minds faster.

section: How to present a storage decision
title: Present storage decisions: lead with requirements, show numbers
body: A storage decision affects many teams for many years, so how you present it matters as much as the decision. First, lead with the requirement, not the product: 'We need 20,000 writes per second per region, a p99 under 10 ms, and 7-year retention' is a sentence everyone can check, while 'We should use Cassandra' is a sentence everyone can argue with. Second, show the numbers: capacity, durability and cost estimates, with assumptions labelled.
deeper:
Leading with requirements changes the conversation from preferences to facts. Reviewers can confirm or challenge each number, and once the requirements are agreed, the product choice often follows naturally. Opening with a product name invites everyone's favourite alternative and turns the review into a debate about technologies instead of needs.

Showing the numbers works for a subtle reason the chapter spells out: reviewers trust a wrong estimate with clear assumptions more than a vague claim, because they can fix the assumptions. If you assume 10 percent of users upload daily and a reviewer knows it is 15 percent, they correct one input and the analysis still stands. A vague claim like 'it will scale' cannot be corrected, only doubted.

The photo capacity sketch in Part 3 is a model of this style: every assumption labelled, simple arithmetic, and a conclusion that follows from the numbers.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter say reviewers trust a wrong estimate with clear assumptions more than a vague claim?
quiz.a: Because they can see and correct the assumptions, so the analysis can be fixed; a vague claim offers nothing to check or repair.

section: How to present a storage decision
title: Present storage decisions: name the trade-off, show the exit
body: Two more rules for presenting a storage decision. Name what you give up: every storage choice sacrifices something, whether consistency, cost, latency, flexibility or operational simplicity, and saying it first shows you understood the trade. Show the exit: explain how data would be moved out if the choice turns out wrong. The chapter notes that showing the exit lowers the stakes of the decision and speeds up approval.
deeper:
Naming the downside first builds credibility. Reviewers who spot an unmentioned weakness will doubt everything else in the proposal; a presenter who lists it upfront demonstrates that the trade was made deliberately. The trade-off catalog in Part 6 is essentially a vocabulary for this step: every row has an option A and B, each with conditions under which it wins.

Showing the exit reframes a scary, irreversible-looking decision as a reversible one. If a clear path exists to migrate away, via an abstraction layer, CDC, open formats and versioned records, then choosing wrong costs a migration rather than a disaster. Reviewers can approve faster because the downside is bounded.

This mirrors the senior staff lens from Part 1, 'how would we leave this system?', and the design-doc checklist's migration section, which includes how we would leave this system later.

quiz.q: How does showing 'the exit' help get a storage decision approved?
quiz.a: It shows the choice is reversible via a migration path, bounding the downside of being wrong, which lowers the stakes and speeds approval.

title: Strong design answers share one shape
body: The chapter closes with ten system-design interview problems, each answered with a model outline rather than the only right answer. A strong answer follows a consistent shape: state the requirements, make estimates, present a design, walk through failure modes, and discuss trade-offs. The key takeaways note that interview answers and real designs share this shape, so practising it builds the same muscle used in production design docs and reviews.
deeper:
Each step has a purpose. Requirements pin down what matters, for example strong read-after-write consistency or active-active writes, and interviewers often reward clarifying questions, as problem 3 does with 'must writes be accepted in every region?'. Estimates size the problem so choices are grounded: problem 5 computes that 50 PB at 100 Gbps takes about 46 days, which changes the plan from weeks to months. The design should separate concerns, such as front end, metadata and data services. Failure modes show operational maturity: region loss, hot objects, deletes during migration. Trade-offs show judgment: what the design gives up and when an alternative would win.

This mirrors the design-doc checklist in Part 4 in compressed form: goals and access patterns, capacity plan, durability math, failure modes, and alternatives considered. It also mirrors how to present a decision: lead with requirements, show the numbers, and name what you give up.

quiz.q: What five elements does the chapter say a strong system-design answer should contain?
quiz.a: Requirements, estimates, a design, failure modes, and trade-offs, the same shape real storage designs share.

title: S3-like object store: front end, metadata, data service
body: To design an S3-like object store supporting PUT, GET, DELETE and LIST by prefix with an 11 nines durability target and strong read-after-write consistency, split it into three parts. A stateless front end handles API servers, authentication and routing. A metadata service maps bucket and key to object locations in a sharded, replicated key-value store, range-partitioned by (bucket, key) so LIST works. A data service of storage nodes stores chunks: large objects are split and erasure-coded, for example RS(10,4), across failure domains.
deeper:
The split mirrors the metadata mental model: bytes and metadata scale differently, so they get separate systems. The front end is stateless so it scales horizontally and any server can handle any request.

Range partitioning by (bucket, key) keeps keys sorted, so listing a prefix is a scan over adjacent keys on one or a few shards rather than a scatter to every shard. Hash partitioning would spread load better but make prefix LIST expensive.

In the data service, large objects are chunked and erasure-coded across failure domains for durability at about 1.4x overhead. Small objects are handled differently: they can be replicated, or packed into larger files to save metadata, which was Haystack's idea. Packing avoids one metadata record and one set of fragments per tiny object, addressing the small-file problem. Chunks, fixed-size pieces of an object, also let reads and repairs work in parallel across many nodes.

quiz.q: Why does the S3-like design range-partition metadata by (bucket, key) instead of hashing it?
quiz.a: Range partitioning keeps keys sorted so LIST by prefix scans adjacent keys on few shards; hashing would scatter a prefix across all shards.

title: S3-like store: metadata commit is the linearization point
body: In the S3-like design, the write path writes data fragments first, then commits metadata. The metadata commit is the linearization point, the single instant the write becomes visible, which gives read-after-write consistency. Background processes maintain health: scrubbers verify checksums, repair workers rebuild lost fragments in parallel, and a garbage collector removes chunks no metadata references. Trade-offs: range partitioning creates hot prefixes, so shards must split automatically; erasure coding cuts cost but makes small reads and repair more expensive.
deeper:
Why data first, metadata second? If metadata were committed first, a reader could find a pointer to fragments that do not yet exist. Writing fragments first means that once metadata commits, the object is fully readable, and any reader after that commit sees the new version. Linearizability, where every operation appears to happen at one instant in real-time order, comes from making that one commit atomic.

The order has a side effect: if a write crashes after storing fragments but before metadata, those fragments are orphaned. The garbage collector handles this by reclaiming unreferenced chunks, alongside chunks from deleted objects.

Scrubbers read data in the background to catch silent corruption before a repair needs it. Parallel repair workers keep the repair window short, which the durability model says drives loss probability.

Hot prefixes arise because sorted keys cluster: many clients writing keys with the same prefix, such as a date, hit one shard, so shards must split automatically as load rises.

quiz.q: In the S3-like design, why are data fragments written before the metadata commit?
quiz.a: So that once metadata commits (the linearization point) the object is fully readable; committing metadata first could expose pointers to missing data. Orphans are garbage-collected.

title: Photo storage for 1B users: CDN, cache, then object store
body: Designing photo storage for 1 billion users starts from Part 3's estimate of about 250 TB per day logical, with reads dominated by recent and viral photos. An upload service writes the original to an object store, then an async pipeline makes resized versions. Metadata, including owner, time, privacy and the location of each size, lives in a sharded database keyed by photo ID. Serving goes through a CDN, then an origin cache, then the object store.
deeper:
Writing the original first and resizing asynchronously keeps uploads fast and durable: the user's photo is safe as soon as the original lands, and resizes can be retried or regenerated later because they are derived data.

Separating metadata from blobs follows the object store pattern. The sharded metadata database answers questions like 'who owns this photo, who can see it, and where is each size stored?' without touching the large blobs, and keying by photo ID spreads load evenly.

The serving path has layers because read popularity is extremely skewed. The CDN absorbs the bulk of reads near users, especially for viral photos; the origin cache catches what the CDN misses; the object store serves the long tail of older photos. Each layer shields the next, so the durable store is sized for misses rather than peak traffic. This combination of immutable blobs, erasure coding and CDN caching is why the chapter's reference table says photos suit this architecture so well.

quiz.q: Why does the photo design generate resized versions asynchronously after writing the original?
quiz.a: The original is durable immediately so uploads stay fast; resized copies are derived data that can be retried or regenerated later.

title: Photo storage: tier hot to wide EC, soft-delete, CDN absorbs virality
body: For tiering, the photo design replicates hot data for fast reads in the first days, then re-encodes it to wider erasure codes, which is what Meta did going from Haystack to f4 and later inside Tectonic. Deletion is soft in metadata immediately, so the photo disappears, with physical deletion by compaction later within the compliance window. For failures, the CDN absorbs a viral photo's hot object, and fragments or replicas span regions for durability.
deeper:
Re-encoding to wider codes as photos cool reduces storage overhead further once fast reads no longer matter; wider codes spread more fragments and save bytes, at the cost of more expensive reads and repairs, which is acceptable for rarely read data.

The two-step delete balances user experience, safety and compliance. Marking the metadata deleted makes the photo vanish instantly for users. Physically reclaiming bytes, often packed inside large files or erasure-coded stripes, happens later during compaction, which rewrites files without deleted entries. The compliance window bounds how late that can be.

A viral photo is a hot key problem, and the CDN solves it by serving copies from edge caches. Region loss is handled by spreading fragments or replicas across regions. There is one accepted weakness: the CDN may serve stale privacy settings for a short time after a user changes them, unless the design explicitly invalidates cached copies. Naming that gap is part of a strong answer.

quiz.q: What consistency weakness does the photo design accept, and how can it be addressed?
quiz.a: After a privacy change, the CDN may briefly serve photos under stale privacy settings; explicit CDN invalidation fixes it.

title: Multi-region KV store: home region, multi-leader, or global consensus
body: Designing a key-value store with multi-region replication starts by clarifying whether writes must be accepted in every region. Option A, home region per key: a single leader per shard in the key's home region using Raft or Paxos, with async replicas elsewhere for local reads; simple and consistent per key. Option B, multi-leader: every region accepts writes and resolves conflicts with last-writer-wins or CRDTs. Option C, global consensus: Paxos across regions per shard, Spanner style.
deeper:
Each option trades differently. Option A gives per-key consistency with local write latency in the home region; a region loss means failover with a small RPO, since async replicas may miss the last writes.

Option B is always writable, even during partitions, but concurrent updates to the same key can lose data under last-writer-wins, where the higher timestamp simply overwrites the other. CRDTs, conflict-free replicated data types, merge concurrent updates without coordination but only work for data types designed for it. Dynamo and Cassandra follow this family.

Option C provides strong consistency across regions because every write is agreed by a majority of regions, but write latency includes a cross-region round trip.

Under the hood, each node runs an LSM tree, and data is partitioned by consistent hashing or by range with automatic splitting. The chapter's recommendation: pick A for most products, B for always-writable carts or presence, and C for money and uniqueness constraints.

quiz.q: In a multi-region KV store, when would you choose a home-region design over multi-leader?
quiz.a: When per-key consistency and simple reasoning matter more than writing in every region during a partition; multi-leader fits always-writable data that tolerates conflict resolution.

title: GDPR deletion: a data inventory and a deletion orchestrator
body: When a user asks to be deleted, their data sits in databases, caches, object stores, search indexes, logs, the lake, ML training sets and backups. GDPR Article 17 requires erasure without undue delay, and companies set internal deadlines. The design starts with a data inventory: every dataset declares whether it has personal data and which column holds the user ID, and 'no declaration, no deploy'. A deletion orchestrator then writes a durable job, fans out to every registered store, tracks completion and retries.
deeper:
The inventory is the foundation because you cannot delete what you cannot find. Making declaration a deploy gate turns it from a voluntary spreadsheet into an enforced contract: a new dataset cannot launch without saying whether it holds personal data and how to find a user's rows.

The orchestrator handles the fan-out reliably. Writing the request as a durable job means a crash does not lose it. Fanning out to every registered store, tracking per-store completion, and retrying failures turns deletion into a trackable workflow rather than a best-effort script. Retries require that each store's delete be idempotent, so repeating it is safe.

Meta's DELF system, published at USENIX Security 2020, is the chapter's example of framework-driven deletion: deletion logic declared as part of the data framework so it is not left to each team to remember. Online stores then simply delete by key, and caches are invalidated.

quiz.q: Why does the GDPR design make dataset declaration a deploy gate ('no declaration, no deploy')?
quiz.a: You cannot delete what you cannot find; enforcing declaration of personal data and the user-ID column guarantees every store is registered for deletion fan-out.

title: GDPR deletion in lakes and backups: row deletes and crypto-shredding
body: Deleting from the lake and backups is the hard part. Lake tables should be partitioned or indexed by user so deletes are row-level, using Iceberg or Hudi deletes plus compaction, not full rewrites. Backups and logs use crypto-shredding: each user's data is encrypted with a per-user key, and deleting the key makes every copy unreadable, including backups, without rewriting them. Periodic scanners then verify by looking for deleted IDs and alerting.
deeper:
Why not just rewrite? Lake files are immutable and large; deleting one user's rows from an unpartitioned table could mean rewriting petabytes. Organizing by user localizes the rewrite, and Iceberg or Hudi record deletes that compaction later applies physically.

Backups are even harder: they are often immutable by design, stored offline, and deliberately hard to modify. Crypto-shredding sidesteps this by making the data meaningless rather than removing it. Destroying the key is a small, fast operation, and it covers every copy at once.

Verification closes the loop: scanners look for supposedly deleted IDs across stores and alert if any remain, catching stores that missed the fan-out.

The trade-offs are named explicitly: per-user keys add key-management load, since there may be a billion keys to store, protect and serve, and deleting from immutable formats needs a compaction budget. The trade-off catalog's customer-managed key option exists for exactly this crypto-shredding use.

quiz.q: How does crypto-shredding help with GDPR deletion in backups?
quiz.a: Each user's data is encrypted with a per-user key; deleting the key makes every copy, including backups, unreadable without rewriting them.

title: Migrating 50 PB: the math says months, not weeks
body: Migrating 50 PB between storage systems with zero downtime begins with an estimate. At 100 Gbps sustained, 50 PB takes about 50e15 times 8 divided by 1e11, which is 4 million seconds or about 46 days. And that assumes perfect, uninterrupted throughput. So the chapter's conclusion is to plan for months, and to plan for bandwidth limits. This single calculation reshapes the whole project, from a quick copy into a long-running dual-system operation.
deeper:
The arithmetic: 50 PB is 50 times 10 to the 15 bytes; times 8 gives bits, 4 times 10 to the 17; divided by 100 Gbps, 10 to the 11 bits per second, gives 4 million seconds, about 46 days.

Real migrations rarely sustain full link speed. Transfer shares bandwidth with production traffic, must be throttled to protect users, pauses for verification and retries, and often competes with repair and replication. So 46 days is a floor, not an estimate of the calendar.

That duration drives the design. Over months, the data being migrated keeps changing: users write, update and delete. A stop-the-world copy is impossible with zero downtime, so the plan must keep both systems in sync while the copy proceeds. That is why the chapter's migration plan uses a routing layer, dual writes, backfill, verification and gradual cutover. It also shows why the day-one migration habits, CDC and versioned records especially, pay off.

quiz.q: Why does the 50 PB migration estimate lead to a plan with dual writes and gradual cutover instead of a simple copy?
quiz.a: Even at full 100 Gbps it takes about 46 days, realistically months, during which data keeps changing, so both systems must stay in sync with zero downtime.

title: Zero-downtime migration in eight steps
body: The chapter's migration plan has eight steps. One, put a routing layer in front so clients do not know which system serves a key. Two, dual write new data to both systems, or write to new and read-through to old. Three, backfill old data in batches, oldest and coldest first. Four, verify with per-object checksums and per-prefix counts. Five, shadow read from both and log mismatches. Six, cut over reads gradually. Seven, keep the old system read-only for rollback. Eight, decommission.
deeper:
This is the pattern Meta used for MyRocks, Uber for its move to GCP, and Dropbox for Magic Pocket (Chapter 13).

The routing layer is what makes the rest possible; it is why the chapter recommends an abstraction layer from day one. Backfilling oldest and coldest data first moves the least-contended data while the new system proves itself. Verification uses checksums for content and counts to catch missing objects. Shadow reads, reading both systems and comparing, find logic bugs before users see them; running a new system on real traffic without users seeing its results is also called a dark launch. Cutover proceeds by percentage of keys or tenants, so problems affect a small slice. Keeping the old system read-only provides a rollback path.

Two failure modes need care. Deletes during migration must be replayed to the new system, or deleted data reappears. Mutations to already-copied objects must be caught using CDC or version checks, so a stale backfilled copy does not overwrite newer data.

quiz.q: During a large migration, what two failure modes must be handled and how?
quiz.a: Deletes during migration must be replayed to the new system; mutations to already-copied objects must be caught via CDC or version checks.

title: Tiering policy: follow the access curve, respect size floors
body: A tiering policy needs inputs: access logs per object or prefix, object size, cost per tier including storage, retrieval and minimum duration, and latency needs. The policy: keep objects in a hot tier for the first N days, where N is the knee of the access curve; move to warm after that; move to cold or archive after M days without reads. Never tier objects below a size floor, respect minimum storage durations, and allow pinning for known-hot data and legal hold.
deeper:
The knee of the access curve is where read rates drop sharply, the natural boundary between hot and warm that the temperature mental model describes.

The exceptions are where naive policies lose money. Small objects can cost more to tier than they save because per-object overhead, such as transition requests and metadata, can exceed the storage savings. Cold tiers often charge minimum storage durations, so deleting or moving an object too early triggers early delete fees. Pinning keeps known-hot objects, such as a popular asset, out of slow tiers, and legal hold prevents deletion or modification for legal reasons regardless of age.

Cost per tier must include retrieval: a cold tier with cheap storage but expensive reads is a bad deal for data that is still read occasionally. The chapter's companion question in design reviews, 'What share of stored data has not been read in 90 days?', provides the evidence to set M.

quiz.q: Why should a tiering policy skip objects below a size floor?
quiz.a: For small objects, per-object overhead of tiering (transition requests, metadata) can exceed the storage savings, so tiering them loses money.

title: Tiering math: move only if savings beat transition plus retrieval
body: Tiering saves money only if the storage saving per month times the months stored is greater than the transition cost plus the expected retrieval cost. If an object will be read back often, or deleted soon, the move may cost more than it saves. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automates this decision per object by watching access. Explicit lifecycle rules are better when you already know the lifecycle, because you avoid monitoring overhead and act on known patterns.
deeper:
The inequality makes the hidden costs explicit. Transition cost is what you pay to move the object: request charges and sometimes rewriting. Expected retrieval cost is the probability of reading the object back times the price of retrieval from the colder tier, which can be high for archival classes. Months stored is limited by retention: if the object will be deleted in two months, a tier saving a small amount per month cannot pay back a larger transition fee, and minimum-duration charges may apply.

The automatic versus explicit choice matches the trade-off catalog: automatic by access when patterns are unknown, explicit by policy when lifecycles are predictable or legal rules apply. For example, log data retained exactly 90 days and rarely read after a week has a known lifecycle, so an explicit rule is simpler and cheaper. User uploads with unpredictable popularity may benefit from per-object automation.

quiz.q: State the chapter's condition for when moving an object to a colder tier saves money.
quiz.a: When monthly storage saving times months stored exceeds the transition cost plus the expected retrieval cost.

title: Profile cache: look-aside, CDC invalidation, leases vs herds
body: A distributed cache for a read-heavy profile service is a look-aside cache keyed by user ID. It is invalidated on write via CDC from the database, not only from the application, so no writer can forget. Leases or request coalescing stop thundering herds on popular keys, as in Meta's memcache paper. Hot keys are replicated, regional pools use cross-region invalidation, and monitoring tracks hit rate and alerts on stale-read rate, not only latency.
deeper:
CDC-driven invalidation is the key robustness idea. If invalidation lives in application code, any service that writes to the database directly, such as a batch job or admin tool, can forget, leaving the cache stale indefinitely. Tailing the database's change stream catches every write regardless of origin.

A thundering herd happens when a popular key expires or is invalidated and thousands of requests miss simultaneously, all hitting the database at once. A lease, a time-limited right to fill the key, lets one requester refresh it while others wait or get the slightly stale value; request coalescing merges concurrent misses into one database read. Meta's 'Scaling Memcache at Facebook' paper (NSDI 2013) describes leases.

Replicating hot keys spreads a celebrity profile's load across several cache nodes. Regional pools keep reads local, with invalidations propagated across regions. Alerting on stale-read rate matters because a cache can be fast and wrong; latency dashboards will not show it.

quiz.q: Why should cache invalidation for the profile service come from database CDC rather than only from application code?
quiz.a: Any writer (batch jobs, other services) could forget to invalidate; CDC sees every database change, so no write can leave the cache stale.

title: Chat storage: conversation partitions and per-conversation sequence
body: For chat message storage, the partition key is the conversation ID and the clustering key is message time or a sequence number. Writes append to an LSM-based store and replicate within the region using quorum writes. Per-conversation sequence numbers from a single leader provide ordering. Recent messages are cached and old messages tiered to cheaper storage. With end-to-end encryption, the server stores only ciphertext, so search must happen on the device.
deeper:
Each choice follows from the access pattern. Partitioning by conversation puts every read on one partition; clustering by sequence makes 'latest messages' a sequential range scan.

LSM stores suit chat's heavy write load. Quorum writes, where a minimum number of replicas must acknowledge, such as W plus R greater than N, keep writes durable and readable within the region even if a replica is slow or down.

Ordering needs a single authority. Timestamps from different devices or servers can disagree, so messages could appear out of order; a single leader per conversation assigning sequence numbers gives every participant the same order.

Chat access is strongly skewed toward recent messages, so caching recent ones and tiering old ones follows the temperature model.

End-to-end encryption changes what the server can do. Because it only holds ciphertext, it cannot build a search index over message content, so search must run on the user's device where plaintext exists. This is a product trade-off imposed by the security model.

quiz.q: Why must search happen on the device when chat messages are end-to-end encrypted?
quiz.a: The server stores only ciphertext and cannot read message content, so it cannot index it; only the device has plaintext to search.

title: Log pipeline: Kafka to Parquet on object storage via Iceberg
body: In the log and event pipeline, producers write to Kafka, which is durable and ordered per partition. Consumers write compressed Parquet files to object storage every few minutes, committed as Iceberg snapshots. Small files are compacted into large ones. Data is partitioned by date and event type. Retention keeps raw events for 30 to 90 days and aggregates longer. Personal fields are tokenized or kept in separate columns so they can be deleted.
deeper:
Kafka decouples producers from storage: bursty producers write to a durable log, and consumers batch at their own pace. Writing Parquet every few minutes balances freshness against file count. Committing each batch as an Iceberg snapshot makes it appear atomically to readers, so queries never see half-written data.

Frequent small writes create the small-file problem: many tiny Parquet files hurt scan performance and metadata load. Compaction merges them into large files in the background.

Partitioning by date and event type lets queries skip irrelevant data and makes retention easy, since dropping an old date partition deletes a day at once.

Tiered retention reflects value over time: raw events are expensive and mostly useful for recent debugging, while aggregates are small and valuable for long-term trends. Tokenizing or isolating personal fields means GDPR deletion can null out or drop specific columns rather than rewriting entire events, connecting to the deletion design in problem 4.

quiz.q: Why does the log pipeline tokenize personal fields or keep them in separate columns?
quiz.a: So personal data can be deleted or removed for compliance without rewriting entire event records in immutable files.

title: Billion-file metadata: shard directories by hash of parent ID
body: A metadata service for a billion-file file system separates the namespace, meaning the directory tree, from block locations, and stores both in a sharded, replicated key-value store. Directory entries are sharded by hash of parent ID, so large directories do not all live on one shard, while a rename within a directory stays cheap because the entries share a parent. Clients cache hot directories using leases. This is the Colossus and Tectonic pattern from Chapter 2.
deeper:
Separating namespace from block locations splits two different workloads: namespace operations such as list, stat, create and rename, versus lookups of where a file's data lives. Each can be scaled independently, which is how Colossus and Tectonic escaped the single-master limits of GFS and HDFS, where one machine held all metadata in memory.

Hashing spreads the tree across many shards instead of placing a popular subtree, or a directory with a huge number of children, on one server, which would recreate the single-master bottleneck on a smaller scale. Keying entries by parent ID keeps the common operation of renaming a file inside its directory a local change rather than a cross-shard transaction.

Client caching with leases reduces load for hot directories. A lease is a time-limited right to trust a cached entry, so clients can serve lookups locally until the lease expires or is revoked, without asking the metadata service every time. At a billion files, avoiding repeated lookups for the same hot paths is a large saving.

quiz.q: Why does the billion-file metadata design shard directories by hash of parent ID?
quiz.a: Hashing spreads directories across shards so no large directory or hot subtree overloads one server, while keying by parent keeps in-directory renames cheap.

title: ACID: the four guarantees of a transaction
body: ACID stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability, the guarantees of a database transaction. Atomicity means all of a transaction's writes happen or none do. Consistency means the data moves from one valid state to another. Isolation means concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work. Durability means once committed, the result survives crashes. Relational and distributed SQL databases offer ACID; many key-value stores offer weaker guarantees.
deeper: ACID matters most where partial results are dangerous. The chapter's anti-pattern of application-maintained indexes without transactions is a missing-atomicity bug: data and index are written separately, and a crash between them leaves them inconsistent forever, which pushed Pinterest to TiDB. The trade-off catalog assigns strong, transactional guarantees to money, identity, inventory and uniqueness. The Part 2 flowchart asks 'Need multi-row transactions or joins?' precisely to route such data to relational or distributed SQL stores. Across many machines, atomic commit needs a protocol such as two-phase commit or consensus, which adds latency.

quiz.q: Which ACID property is violated when a crash leaves data written but its index entry missing?
quiz.a: Atomicity: the two related writes should have happened together or not at all.

title: Append-only and immutable data
body: Append-only storage only adds data at the end and never overwrites existing bytes. Immutable data is never changed after being written. Logs, event streams, LSM tree files and photos are typical examples. These properties make storage simpler: no in-place update coordination, easy caching, safe erasure coding and straightforward replication. Changes and deletes are expressed as new records or markers, with space reclaimed later by compaction or garbage collection.
deeper: Immutability runs through the chapter's designs. Photos and videos suit erasure coding and CDN caching because they never change, so cached copies are never stale versions. Kafka logs are append-only and ordered per partition, which makes them good for events and CDC. LSM trees write immutable sorted files (SSTables) and record deletes as tombstones. Lake tables in Parquet and Iceberg are immutable files, which is why GDPR deletion needs row-level deletes plus compaction rather than editing in place, and why deleting from immutable formats needs a compaction budget.

quiz.q: Why does immutability make CDN caching of photos safe?
quiz.a: The object never changes, so a cached copy can never be an outdated version of the bytes.

title: Archival storage: cheapest tier, slow to read
body: Archival storage is the lowest-cost storage tier, for data rarely or never read. It holds frozen data kept for law or insurance, old backups, and records past their active life. The trade-off is access: retrieval is typically slow and may carry fees and minimum storage durations. In the reference architecture, data moves to an archive tier after its retention window instead of staying on expensive storage.
deeper: Archival fits the end of the data lifecycle described in the temperature model: hot, warm, cold, then frozen. The tiering interview problem lists the gotchas that make archival tricky: retrieval cost must be included in the savings calculation, minimum storage durations mean early deletes incur fees, and small objects may cost more to transition than they save. The design-doc Lifecycle section asks when data moves to archival and when it is finally deleted. Archival data still needs an owner and a retention rule; archiving is not a substitute for deleting data nobody needs.

quiz.q: Why should retrieval cost be considered before moving data to archival storage?
quiz.a: Archival tiers are cheap to store but costly and slow to read; frequent reads can erase the storage savings.

title: Availability vs durability: answering vs not losing
body: Availability is the fraction of time a system answers requests correctly. Durability is the probability that stored data is not lost. They are different: a system can be unavailable during an outage yet lose nothing, or be available while silently having lost data. Durability depends heavily on repair speed and independent failure domains; availability depends on failover, redundancy of serving paths and blast radius.
deeper: The S3-like interview problem sets an 11 nines durability target, a statement about loss, not uptime. The design-doc checklist separates them: 'Durability math' covers replication or erasure code, failure domains, repair time and annual loss probability, while 'Availability and consistency' covers the SLO, region layout and behaviour during a partition. Choices can trade one for the other: synchronous cross-region replication improves durability against region loss but can reduce write availability if the remote region is unreachable. Mixing the two terms in a design review leads to confused requirements.

quiz.q: Can a storage system be unavailable without losing durability?
quiz.a: Yes. During an outage requests fail, but if data is safely stored it is still durable and returns when service recovers.

title: Object storage, buckets and blobs
body: Object storage is flat key-to-blob storage accessed over HTTP, such as S3 and GCS. A blob is a large binary object with no internal structure the store cares about. A bucket is a top-level container of objects. There are no real directories or in-place edits: you PUT, GET, DELETE and LIST by key prefix. Object storage is cheap per byte and massively scalable, but has higher latency than block or local storage.
deeper: Object storage is the chapter's default for large immutable data: photos, videos and lake files in Parquet and Iceberg. The Part 2 flowchart sends blobs over 1 MB there, and the latency modifier notes object storage fits p99 targets of 100 ms and up. Its weakness is small objects: per-object metadata and per-request costs make billions of tiny objects expensive, so records should be packed into larger files or stored in a key-value store. The S3-like interview design shows the internals: a stateless front end, a metadata service keyed by (bucket, key), and erasure-coded chunks on storage nodes.

quiz.q: Why is object storage a poor fit for billions of tiny records?
quiz.a: Per-object metadata, LIST cost and per-request charges dominate when each object is small.

title: Block storage: a disk over the network
body: Block storage exposes fixed-size blocks, like a disk, to a machine that puts its own file system or database on top. Examples are AWS EBS and Google Persistent Disk. Unlike object storage, blocks can be overwritten in place and read with low latency, which databases need. Block volumes are usually attached to one machine at a time, so they suit a single database or VM rather than shared access by many clients.
deeper: Block, file and object storage are the three classic interfaces. Block is the lowest level: the storage system knows nothing about files or objects, only numbered blocks. That makes it flexible, since any engine can run on it, and fast for random reads and writes, but it pushes all structure and metadata management to the machine using it. In the trade-off catalog's storage-and-compute row, networked block storage is a form of disaggregation: compute and storage scale separately, at the cost of a network hop compared with local disk.

quiz.q: Why do databases typically run on block storage rather than object storage?
quiz.a: Block storage allows low-latency in-place overwrites of small blocks, which database engines need; object storage does not.

title: Bloom filter: 'definitely not' or 'maybe'
body: A Bloom filter is a compact data structure that answers membership questions with either 'definitely not present' or 'maybe present'. It never gives false negatives but can give false positives. It uses far less memory than storing the keys themselves. Storage engines use Bloom filters to skip files or disks that cannot contain a key, avoiding wasted reads and keeping lookups fast even when data is spread across many files.
deeper: The classic use is in LSM trees, which store data across many sorted files (SSTables). A point read might otherwise check every file. A small Bloom filter per file lets the engine skip files that definitely lack the key, reducing read amplification, reading more bytes than requested. The trade-off is memory for the filters and a tunable false-positive rate: more bits per key means fewer wasted reads. Because answers are only 'maybe', a positive result still requires reading the actual data to confirm.

quiz.q: Why is a Bloom filter useful in an LSM tree read path?
quiz.a: It lets reads skip SSTables that definitely lack the key, cutting read amplification; a 'maybe' still requires checking the file.

title: B-tree: the in-place update index
body: A B-tree is a balanced tree index that updates pages in place. Keys are kept sorted in fixed-size pages, and the tree stays shallow, so a lookup needs few page reads. Because each key has one current location, point reads and range scans are fast and predictable. B-trees power most relational databases. The trade-off is that random in-place writes are costlier than the sequential writes of LSM trees.
deeper: The chapter's trade-off catalog says to pick a B-tree for read-heavy workloads with in-place updates and range scans, and an LSM tree for write-heavy workloads, compression and flash. The Part 2 modifiers say heavy overwrites favour B-trees. In-place updates mean a small change rewrites a whole page, contributing to write amplification, physical bytes written divided by logical bytes written. Engines typically pair B-trees with a write-ahead log so a crash mid-update can be recovered. Chapter 5 of the book covers both engines in depth.

quiz.q: What workload does the trade-off catalog assign to B-trees?
quiz.a: Read-heavy workloads with in-place updates and range scans.

title: LSM tree and SSTables
body: A log-structured merge (LSM) tree buffers writes in memory, flushes them as sorted files, and compacts those files in the background. Each flushed file is an SSTable, a sorted string table: an immutable sorted file. Turning random writes into sequential ones makes LSM trees fast for writes, compressible and flash-friendly. Reads may check several SSTables, so engines use Bloom filters and compaction to keep reads efficient.
deeper: LSM trees appear throughout the reference architecture: messages go to LSM-based stores like Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable or MyRocks, and the multi-region KV interview design runs an LSM tree per node. The original paper is O'Neil et al. (1996), listed in the further reading. The cost of LSM trees is compaction work, which consumes CPU and disk bandwidth and causes write amplification as data is rewritten across levels, plus read amplification when a key may live in several files. A write-ahead log protects the in-memory buffer against crashes before flush.

quiz.q: Why are LSM trees good for write-heavy workloads?
quiz.a: They buffer writes in memory and flush sorted immutable files sequentially, avoiding random in-place updates.

title: Compaction and tombstones
body: Compaction merges and rewrites files to drop old versions and deleted data, in LSM trees and in data lakes. Because those systems write immutable files, a delete cannot erase bytes directly; instead it writes a tombstone, a marker recording the delete. Reads treat tombstoned keys as gone. Later, compaction rewrites files without the deleted data, and the tombstone itself can be dropped. Until then, deleted data still occupies disk.
deeper: This matters for both cost and compliance. Deleted data lingers until compaction runs, so physical deletion lags logical deletion. The photo-storage interview design uses exactly this: soft delete in metadata immediately, physical delete by compaction later within the compliance window. The GDPR design uses Iceberg or Hudi deletes plus compaction in the lake, and notes deleting from immutable formats needs compaction budget. The log pipeline compacts many small Parquet files into large ones. Compaction consumes disk and CPU and contributes to write amplification, so it must be scheduled and rate-limited.

quiz.q: Why does a deleted key in an LSM tree still take disk space for a while?
quiz.a: The delete writes a tombstone; the old data is removed only when compaction rewrites the files.

title: Read, write and space amplification
body: Three amplification metrics describe storage engine overhead. Read amplification is reading more bytes than requested, such as checking several files for one key. Write amplification is physical bytes written divided by logical bytes written, from rewrites like compaction or page updates. Space amplification is storing more bytes than the logical data size, from old versions, tombstones or redundancy. Engines trade these against each other.
deeper: B-trees and LSM trees sit at different points. B-trees rewrite whole pages for small changes, raising write amplification, but read efficiently. LSM trees write sequentially but compaction rewrites data repeatedly, and reads may touch several SSTables unless Bloom filters help; uncompacted old versions add space amplification. Redundancy is also a form of space amplification: 3x for triple replication versus 1.4x for RS(10,4). Write amplification especially matters on flash, where it consumes device endurance. Tuning compaction is essentially choosing which amplification to pay.

quiz.q: How does RS(10,4) compare with triple replication in space amplification?
quiz.a: RS(10,4) stores 1.4x the data size; triple replication stores 3x.

title: Cache hit rate and CDNs
body: Cache hit rate is the share of reads served by the cache rather than the backing store. A content delivery network (CDN) is a set of caches near users for static content such as photos and videos. High hit rates shield databases and object stores from load and cut latency. But hit rate alone is not enough: a cache can be fast and wrong, so the chapter says to alert on stale-read rate too.
deeper: In the reference architecture, photos are served through a CDN, then an origin cache, then the object store; each layer reduces load on the next. A viral photo is a hot key, and the CDN absorbs it. The trade-off is freshness: the photo design admits the CDN may serve stale privacy settings unless explicitly invalidated. For the profile cache interview problem, the chapter recommends measuring hit rate and alerting on stale-read rate, not only latency. A drop in hit rate, for example after a cache node dies, instantly increases load on the database.

quiz.q: Why isn't a high cache hit rate sufficient to call a cache healthy?
quiz.a: It can serve stale data quickly; stale-read rate must also be monitored.

title: Checksums and scrubbing catch silent corruption
body: A checksum is a small value computed from data and used to detect corruption: recompute it on read, and a mismatch means the bytes changed. Scrubbing is background reading of stored data to find corruption before anyone needs it. Together they catch silent corruption, where data changes without any error. Checksums should be end-to-end, verified from writer to reader, not just at the disk.
deeper: Replication alone does not help if a corrupt copy is served or copied. The S3-like design runs scrubbers that verify checksums and repair workers that rebuild bad fragments. Design-review question 13 asks: how do we detect silent corruption, and are checksums end-to-end? The blobs-in-database fix keeps a pointer and checksum in the row, so the app can verify the fetched blob. Migrations verify with per-object checksums. Scrubbing finds latent errors early, which matters for durability: a hidden bad fragment effectively reduces how many further failures an object can survive.

quiz.q: Why does a storage system scrub data in the background instead of only checking checksums on read?
quiz.a: Rarely read data could stay corrupt unnoticed; scrubbing finds and repairs it before another failure makes it unrecoverable.

title: Chunks: fixed-size pieces of files and objects
body: A chunk is a fixed-size piece of a file or object. Storage systems split large objects into chunks so the pieces can be spread across many nodes, stored and repaired independently, and read in parallel. Chunks are the unit that gets replicated or erasure-coded and placed across failure domains. Metadata records which chunks make up each object and where they live.
deeper: In the S3-like design, large objects are split into chunks and erasure-coded, for example RS(10,4), across failure domains; a garbage collector later removes chunks no metadata references, such as those left by a crashed write or a deleted object. Chunking enables parallel repair: when a disk dies, its chunks can be rebuilt by many nodes at once, which shortens the repair window, as Dropbox's Magic Pocket does. The trade-off is metadata: smaller chunks mean more entries to track, which is why chunk size is usually large.

quiz.q: How does splitting objects into chunks help durability?
quiz.a: Chunks spread across many nodes can be rebuilt in parallel after a failure, shortening the repair window.

title: Columnar formats and table manifests
body: A columnar format stores each column's values together instead of storing whole rows together. Parquet and ORC are examples. Analytical queries that read a few columns across billions of rows only touch those columns, and similar values compress well. A manifest is a file listing the data files that make up a table snapshot, which is how table formats like Iceberg track which files belong to a table version.
deeper: Columnar formats are why the flowchart sends scans and aggregates to lakes and warehouses. In the log pipeline, consumers write compressed Parquet files every few minutes and commit them as Iceberg snapshots. The manifest is the mechanism: a commit writes new data files, then publishes a new manifest listing them, so readers see either the old table or the new one, never a half-written state. Manifests also let engines skip files using per-file statistics. Because many engines read Parquet and Iceberg, they double as open formats that ease future migrations.

quiz.q: How does an Iceberg-style manifest let readers avoid seeing half-written data?
quiz.a: A snapshot's manifest lists its files; new files become visible only when a new manifest is committed.

title: Consensus and leaders
body: Consensus is a protocol that lets nodes agree on a value despite failures; Paxos and Raft are the standard examples. A leader is the replica that orders writes for a shard. Consensus is typically used to elect the leader and to replicate its log so a majority agrees on each write. Together they give a single, agreed order of writes per key, which is what strong consistency requires.
deeper: The chapter uses these in several designs. The multi-region KV store's option A runs a single leader per shard with Raft or Paxos inside the home region. Option C runs Paxos across regions per shard, Spanner style, giving strong consistency but adding a cross-region round trip to every write. Chat storage uses a single leader per conversation to assign sequence numbers. The Part 2 consistency modifier states that if readers must never see stale data, you need a single leader or consensus per key. The cost is that writes stall when a majority or leader is unreachable.

quiz.q: Why does strong consistency usually require a leader or consensus per key?
quiz.a: Something must impose one agreed order on writes so every read sees the latest committed value.

title: Quorums and read repair
body: A quorum is the minimum number of replicas that must respond to an operation. With N replicas, writes wait for W acknowledgments and reads query R replicas; if W plus R is greater than N, every read overlaps at least one replica holding the latest write. Read repair fixes stale replicas when a read notices that replicas disagree, writing the newest value back to the lagging ones.
deeper: Quorums are the backbone of leaderless designs in the Dynamo and Cassandra family, and the chat storage interview design replicates within a region using quorum writes. Tuning W and R trades latency against consistency: lower values respond faster but risk stale reads. Read repair is one of several anti-entropy mechanisms: it only fixes data that is actually read, so rarely read keys may stay stale until background repair processes reach them. Quorums tolerate slow or failed replicas without a leader, supporting the always-writable option in the trade-off catalog.

quiz.q: Why does W plus R greater than N help reads see the latest write?
quiz.a: The read set and write set must overlap in at least one replica that has the latest acknowledged write.

title: Consistent hashing: move few keys when nodes change
body: Consistent hashing is a hashing scheme that moves only a small fraction of keys when nodes join or leave. Keys and nodes are placed on the same hash space, and each key belongs to the nearest node. Adding a node takes over only a slice of keys from its neighbours, instead of reshuffling almost everything as simple modulo hashing would. It is a standard way to partition key-value stores.
deeper: The multi-region KV interview design partitions by consistent hashing or by range with automatic splitting. Consistent hashing spreads load evenly and makes scaling out cheap, but it destroys key order, so range queries and prefix LIST become expensive. That is why the S3-like design instead range-partitions metadata by (bucket, key), accepting hot prefixes and automatic shard splits. Consistent hashing is used by the Dynamo and Cassandra family. The choice between hash and range partitioning is one of the earliest decisions in a KV design.

quiz.q: What does consistent hashing give up compared with range partitioning?
quiz.a: Key order, so range scans and prefix listing become scatter operations across many nodes.

title: Shards, partitions, resharding and rebalancing
body: A shard is a horizontal slice of a dataset. A partition is a subset of data owned by one group of nodes; confusingly, 'partition' also means a network split. Resharding changes how data is split into shards, for example splitting a hot shard. Rebalancing moves data between nodes to even out load. Good partition keys spread load; bad ones create hot, oversized partitions.
deeper: The unbounded-partition anti-pattern shows what goes wrong: a key like 'country' or 'day' grows without limit until one partition is hot and too large to move. The fix is a high-cardinality key or a bucket suffix. Design-review question 7 asks for the resharding plan and whether it has been tested, because resharding under load is when systems fail. Rebalancing competes with user traffic for bandwidth, much like repair. The other meaning of partition, a network split, appears in design docs: 'what happens during a partition' asks which side keeps accepting writes.

quiz.q: What two meanings does 'partition' have in storage systems?
quiz.a: A subset of data owned by one group of nodes, and a network split that separates nodes.

title: CRDTs and vector clocks
body: A CRDT, conflict-free replicated data type, is a data structure whose concurrent updates merge automatically without coordination, such as a counter or set designed to converge. A vector clock is a set of per-replica counters used to detect concurrent updates: if neither version's clock dominates the other, the updates happened concurrently and must be reconciled. Both help multi-leader systems handle conflicts.
deeper: In the multi-region KV interview problem, option B, multi-leader, resolves conflicts with last-writer-wins timestamps or CRDTs. Last-writer-wins is simple but concurrent updates can lose data, since one write silently overwrites the other. CRDTs avoid that loss for data types they support. Vector clocks, used in the Dynamo lineage, tell the system when two writes truly conflicted rather than one following the other, so it can merge them or surface both to the application. These tools suit always-writable data like shopping carts or presence.

quiz.q: What problem does a vector clock solve in a multi-leader system?
quiz.a: It detects whether two updates were concurrent or ordered, so real conflicts can be reconciled instead of silently overwritten.

title: Data residency: keeping data in allowed regions
body: Data residency is a rule that data must stay in a given country or region, usually because of law or contracts. It constrains where primary copies, replicas, backups, caches and lake copies may live. Residency pinning means the storage system enforces those locations. It interacts directly with replication strategy, since cross-region copies made for durability must stay within allowed regions, and violating residency is a compliance incident, not just a bug.
deeper: The Part 2 compliance modifier lists residency pinning alongside deletion by user ID and per-tenant keys. Design-review question 27 asks which regions data may live in and what enforces it; the enforcement half matters because a policy with no technical control is easily broken by a new replica, backup job or analytics copy. The design-doc compliance section includes residency in its review. Residency also shapes the architecture: a global app may need region-specific stores or tenants rather than one global replicated table.

quiz.q: Why does the review ask what enforces residency, not just which regions are allowed?
quiz.a: Without a technical control, a new replica, backup or analytics copy can silently move data into a forbidden region.

title: Dark launch: real traffic, invisible results
body: A dark launch runs a new system on real production traffic without users seeing its results. The old system still answers users, while the new one processes the same requests in parallel so its behaviour, performance and correctness can be compared. It lets teams find bugs and capacity problems under real load before any user depends on the new system.
deeper: The chapter's migration plan uses the same idea as shadow reads: read from both old and new systems, compare the results and log mismatches, before gradually cutting over reads by percentage of keys or tenants. Dark launching is valuable because synthetic tests rarely reproduce real key distributions, hot keys and odd data. Its cost is running both systems at once, roughly doubling load on shared dependencies, and care that the dark system never causes side effects users can see, such as sending notifications.

quiz.q: What does a dark launch reveal that synthetic testing often misses?
quiz.a: Behaviour under real traffic patterns, including real hot keys and odd data, without users seeing the results.

title: Deduplication: store identical data once
body: Deduplication means storing identical data only once. When multiple files, chunks or objects have the same content, the system keeps one physical copy and points all references at it, often identifying duplicates by a content hash. It can save large amounts of space for backups, file sync and user uploads where the same content appears repeatedly, such as the same file uploaded by many users.
deeper: Deduplication trades space for complexity. The system needs an index of content hashes, which is itself metadata that must scale. Deletion becomes reference counting: a chunk can only be removed when no object references it anymore, which garbage collection must track correctly. Dedup also interacts with compliance and crypto-shredding: data encrypted with per-user keys looks different for each user, so identical content encrypted separately cannot be deduplicated. The design choice depends on how much duplication actually exists.

quiz.q: Why does deduplication complicate deletion?
quiz.a: A shared copy can only be removed when no remaining object references it, so deletes need reference tracking.

title: Egress: the bill for data leaving
body: Egress is data leaving a cloud or region, and it is often billed. Serving large files to users, replicating across regions, or reading cloud data from elsewhere can generate egress charges that rival or exceed the cost of storing the data. A storage cost model that counts only GB-months misses it. CDNs and regional read replicas are common ways to reduce egress on hot read paths.
deeper: The design-doc cost model lists storage, requests, network egress, replication, backup and people. Design-review question 32 asks: what is the egress cost of the main read path? Egress also affects migrations and build-versus-buy decisions: moving petabytes out of a cloud can be expensive, which is part of the price of leaving a system. Cross-region replication by default doubles storage and adds transfer cost for data that may never need it, one reason the chapter warns against it as a default.

quiz.q: Why must a storage cost model include egress?
quiz.a: Data leaving a cloud or region is billed and can rival storage cost on read-heavy or cross-region paths.

title: Strong vs eventual consistency, and linearizability
body: Strong consistency means every read sees the latest committed write. Eventual consistency means replicas converge if writes stop, but reads in the meantime may be stale. Linearizability is the strictest form of strong consistency: every operation appears to happen at one instant in real-time order. Stronger guarantees make applications simpler to reason about but cost latency and availability, especially across regions.
deeper: The trade-off catalog assigns strong consistency to money, identity, inventory and uniqueness, and eventual consistency to feeds, counters, caches and analytics. The S3-like design achieves read-after-write by making the metadata commit the linearization point, the instant the write takes effect. Eventual consistency enables always-writable multi-leader systems but requires conflict resolution. Cross-region strong consistency, as in Spanner-style global consensus, adds a cross-region round trip to writes. Choosing the weakest guarantee a dataset can tolerate is often the cheapest improvement available.

quiz.q: Give one workload suited to eventual consistency and one requiring strong consistency.
quiz.a: Eventual: feeds, counters, caches or analytics. Strong: money, identity, inventory or uniqueness constraints.

title: Snapshots and snapshot isolation
body: A snapshot is a point-in-time view of data. Snapshot isolation is a transaction isolation level where each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot, so it never sees other transactions' partial writes, even as data changes underneath. Snapshots support backups, table versions in lake formats like Iceberg, and consistent reads during long-running queries, without blocking writers. Readers see a stable view while new writes continue to arrive.
deeper: Snapshots appear across the chapter. The log pipeline commits Parquet files as Iceberg snapshots, each described by a manifest listing the table's files, so readers get a consistent table version. Backups are snapshots taken over time, which is why they protect against mistakes that replication would copy instantly. Snapshot isolation is common in databases because it lets readers and writers proceed concurrently. It is weaker than full serializability: certain anomalies between concurrent transactions remain possible, which matters for invariants like uniqueness.

quiz.q: Why do snapshots protect against operator mistakes when replication does not?
quiz.a: Replication copies a bad write or delete instantly; a snapshot preserves the earlier point-in-time state to restore from.

title: Failure domains, zones and regions
body: A failure domain is a set of components that can fail together, such as a rack, a zone or a region. A zone is an isolated data center or group within a region.
