A region is a geographic area with several data centers. Durability math assumes copies fail independently, which is only true if copies sit in different failure domains. Placing all replicas in one rack defeats redundancy.
deeper: Design-review question 12 asks how many failures a single item can survive and whether copies are in independent failure domains. The S3-like design erasure-codes chunks across failure domains. The design-doc failure-mode section walks through disk, node, rack, zone and region loss, each with detection, impact and recovery. Wider failure domains give better protection but cost more: spreading copies across regions means cross-region bandwidth, latency for synchronous writes, and egress, while spreading across zones within a region is usually a cheaper middle ground.

quiz.q: Why doesn't three-way replication guarantee durability if all copies are in one rack?
quiz.a: The rack is a single failure domain; one rack failure can destroy all three copies at once.

title: Fsync and the write-ahead log
body: Fsync is the system call that forces data to durable media rather than leaving it in memory buffers. A write-ahead log (WAL) records changes before they are applied to the main data structures. Together they provide crash safety: a database appends the change to its WAL, fsyncs it, then acknowledges the write. After a crash, replaying the log restores any change that was acknowledged.
deeper: Without fsync, the operating system may report a write as complete while the data sits in volatile cache; a power loss then loses acknowledged writes. Fsync is slow relative to memory writes, so engines batch many changes into one fsync, called group commit, trading a little latency for throughput. B-tree engines use a WAL so a crash mid-page-update can be repaired, and LSM trees use one to protect the in-memory buffer before it is flushed. CDC streams are often built by reading the WAL.

quiz.q: Why does a database fsync its write-ahead log before acknowledging a write?
quiz.a: So the change is on durable media; after a crash, replaying the log recovers every acknowledged write.

title: Garbage collection: reclaiming unreferenced data
body: Garbage collection reclaims space from deleted or unreferenced data. In storage systems, data is often not removed at the moment it is deleted or orphaned; a background process later finds chunks, files or versions that nothing references anymore and frees them. It keeps storage from filling with leftovers from deletes, crashed writes and overwritten versions, which would otherwise be paid for indefinitely.
deeper: In the S3-like design, writes store data fragments first and commit metadata second; a crash between the two leaves unreferenced fragments, and the garbage collector removes them along with chunks from deleted objects. Garbage collection must be careful: deleting a chunk that is still referenced is data loss, so collectors often wait a grace period and double-check references. That delay also works like soft delete, giving a window to recover from mistakes. Like compaction, it consumes I/O and must be rate-limited.

quiz.q: Why must a garbage collector be conservative about what it deletes?
quiz.a: Removing a chunk that is still referenced destroys live data, so it waits and verifies nothing points to it.

title: Hot keys: when one key gets most of the traffic
body: A hot key is a key receiving far more traffic than others, such as a celebrity profile, a viral photo or today's date partition. Because a key lives on one shard, all that traffic lands on one set of nodes, which can saturate while the rest of the cluster sits idle. Adding more nodes does not help unless the hot key's load is spread or absorbed.
deeper: The chapter offers several remedies. Caches and CDNs absorb reads: a viral photo is served from CDN edges. The profile cache replicates hot keys across nodes and uses leases or request coalescing to stop thundering herds when a popular key expires. For write hot spots from bad partition keys, add a bucket suffix or pick a higher-cardinality key. Design-review question 2 asks what the hottest key is and its peak QPS, and the design-doc failure modes list includes hot key, because averages hide skew.

quiz.q: Why doesn't adding nodes fix a hot key?
quiz.a: A key lives on one shard, so its traffic still hits the same nodes; load must be spread by caching, replication or key redesign.

title: Idempotent operations make retries safe
body: An idempotent operation has the same effect whether it runs once or many times. Deleting a key, or setting a value to a fixed number, is idempotent; appending to a list or incrementing a counter is not. Idempotency matters because distributed systems retry: a timeout does not tell you whether the operation happened, so retrying must not cause double effects.
deeper: The GDPR deletion orchestrator in the chapter fans out to every registered store, tracks completion and retries; those retries are safe only if each store's delete is idempotent. Migrations replay deletes and changes to the new system, and backfills may copy the same object twice; version checks keep repeated writes from overwriting newer data. Non-idempotent operations can often be made safe with unique request IDs, so a store recognizes and ignores duplicates.

quiz.q: Why should the GDPR deletion fan-out use idempotent deletes?
quiz.a: The orchestrator retries failed or uncertain deletes; idempotency makes repeating them harmless.

title: IOPS and tail latency
body: IOPS is input/output operations per second, a measure of how many reads and writes a device or system can handle. Tail latency is high-percentile latency such as p99, the time within which 99 percent of requests complete. Storage systems often run out of IOPS before capacity, and users feel tail latency more than averages, especially when one page load triggers many storage requests.
deeper: Design-review question 8 asks which resource runs out first: IOPS, capacity, CPU, memory or metadata. A dataset of many small, randomly accessed items may exhaust a disk's IOPS while most of its capacity sits empty. The Part 2 latency modifier maps p99 targets to media: under 1 ms needs memory or local flash, under 10 ms SSD-backed key-value storage, 100 ms and up allows object storage. DynamoDB's single primary goal, predictable p99 latency, shows how central tail latency is. Background work like repair, compaction and noisy tenants mostly hurts the tail.

quiz.q: Why can a storage system run out of IOPS while disks still have free capacity?
quiz.a: Many small random reads and writes exhaust the device's operations per second long before its bytes fill up.

title: Leases: time-limited rights
body: A lease is a time-limited right granted to one party, used for leaders and cache fills. A leader lease lets one node act as leader until the lease expires, so a partitioned old leader stops acting on its own. A cache-fill lease lets one client refresh a missing key while others wait. Because leases expire automatically, a crashed holder cannot block everyone forever.
deeper: The chapter uses leases in two interview designs. The profile cache uses leases or request coalescing to stop thundering herds on popular keys, following Meta's memcache paper (NSDI 2013): only the lease holder queries the database after a miss. The billion-file metadata service lets clients cache hot directories with leases, so they can trust cached entries until the lease expires. The trade-off is timing: short leases mean more renewal traffic, long leases mean slower recovery when a holder dies, and leases rely on reasonably synchronized clocks.

quiz.q: Why do leases expire automatically rather than lasting until released?
quiz.a: If the holder crashes or is partitioned, the right lapses on its own, so others are not blocked forever.

title: Legal hold, object lock and WORM
body: Legal hold is a block on deletion for legal reasons, such as litigation. Object lock is WORM protection that prevents deletion of objects for a set period. WORM means write once, read many: data can be written and read but not modified or deleted. These controls override normal retention and deletion, protecting data from mistakes, malicious deletes and bugs, and meeting legal requirements.
deeper: Design-review question 15 asks whether an operator or a bug can delete everything and what stops it; object lock is one of the named answers, alongside soft delete and delayed purge. Legal hold appears in the design-doc compliance section and in the tiering policy, which must allow pinning for legal hold. These controls create tension with deletion obligations: GDPR requires erasure without undue delay, but a legal hold can require keeping specific data, so the deletion orchestrator must know which holds apply before it deletes.

quiz.q: How does object lock protect against a buggy mass delete?
quiz.a: WORM protection blocks deletion for a set period, so even an operator or bug cannot remove the locked objects.

title: Multi-tenancy: many customers, one system
body: Multi-tenancy means many customers, or tenants, share one system. It improves utilization because spare capacity is pooled, but it creates noisy-neighbour risk: one tenant's heavy workload can slow everyone else. Safe multi-tenant storage needs per-tenant quotas, priority classes, and often per-tenant encryption keys so one tenant's data can be isolated or revoked. Without these controls, pooling capacity also pools failure.
deeper: The chapter's anti-pattern of one giant shared cluster with no quotas shows the danger: a tenant's batch job saturates disks and every online service slows down. Meta's Tectonic is multi-tenant by design and uses traffic classes to prevent this. Azure stamps and AWS cells limit how many tenants any failure touches. Design-review question 28 asks whether a single tenant's key can be revoked, and the trade-off catalog notes customer-managed keys enable per-tenant revocation and crypto-shredding.

quiz.q: What protections does shared multi-tenant storage need?
quiz.a: Per-tenant quotas and priority classes to contain noisy neighbours, plus isolation such as per-tenant keys.

title: Namespaces: the set of names
body: A namespace is the set of names in a storage system: file paths in a file system, or keys in an object store or key-value store. Namespace operations include create, list, rename and stat. Managing the namespace is a metadata problem, and at billions of names it often becomes the bottleneck, independent of how many bytes the system stores. A system can have plenty of disk left and still fail because its namespace service is overloaded.
deeper: The billion-file metadata interview design separates the namespace, the directory tree, from block locations, and stores both in a sharded key-value store, the Colossus and Tectonic pattern. Directory renames and listings are the tricky namespace operations: a rename that crosses shards needs coordination, while a list over a huge directory must not overload one server. Object stores simplify the namespace to a flat key space with prefix listing, which is why the S3-like design range-partitions keys by (bucket, key).

quiz.q: Why is namespace management considered a metadata problem rather than a capacity problem?
quiz.a: It depends on how many names and namespace operations exist, not on how many bytes are stored.

title: Replication factor: how many full copies
body: Replication factor is the number of full copies of data a system keeps; 3 is the classic choice. Higher replication factors survive more simultaneous failures and serve more reads, but multiply storage cost: a replication factor of 3 means 3x the raw bytes. Erasure coding can give equal or better fault tolerance at far lower overhead, at the cost of more expensive reads and repairs.
deeper: The chapter's durability model shows why copy count is not the whole story: with three replicas, data is lost only if the other two fail during the repair window, so repair speed matters as much as adding copies. RS(10,4) tolerates 4 failures at 1.4x overhead, versus 2 failures at 3x for triple replication. Hence the trade-off catalog rule: replicate hot, small, latency-sensitive data; erasure-code warm or cold, large objects. Derived data may use a lower replication factor because it can be rebuilt.

quiz.q: How many failures does triple replication tolerate compared with RS(10,4)?
quiz.a: Triple replication tolerates 2 failures at 3x overhead; RS(10,4) tolerates 4 at 1.4x.

title: RPO and RTO: how much loss, how long down
body: RPO, the recovery point objective, is how much data you may lose in a disaster, measured in time, such as the last 5 seconds of writes. RTO, the recovery time objective, is how long recovery may take. Together they define disaster recovery requirements. An RPO of zero requires synchronous replication to another location; a short RTO requires fast failover and tested restores.
deeper: The chapter uses RPO to decide cross-region replication: synchronous when RPO must be zero, asynchronous when latency matters more than the last seconds of data. The anti-pattern list says synchronous replication should be an explicit per-dataset choice backed by an RPO requirement. Design-review question 19 asks what happens to in-flight writes when a region is lost and what the RPO is. The multi-region KV home-region design accepts a small RPO on failover. RTO connects to backups: a backup that takes days to restore may miss the RTO, which only a restore drill reveals.

quiz.q: What RPO forces synchronous cross-region replication?
quiz.a: An RPO of zero, meaning no acknowledged writes may be lost if a region fails.

title: Secondary indexes
body: A secondary index is an index on a field other than the primary key, such as finding users by email when the table is keyed by user ID. Secondary indexes make more queries fast but cost extra writes and storage, and must stay consistent with the data. Whether a store maintains them transactionally, updating index and data together, is a key selection criterion.
deeper: The reference architecture puts profiles in SQL-style stores partly because they need secondary indexes and updates. Design-review question 3 asks which queries need a secondary index and whether it is transactional with the data. When a store lacks built-in indexes, teams build their own with separate writes, and the chapter's anti-pattern shows the result: a crash between data and index writes leaves them inconsistent forever, which was a key reason Pinterest moved its graph store to TiDB. In partitioned stores, a secondary index may span every shard, making it costlier to keep consistent.

quiz.q: Why is a store's support for transactional secondary indexes an important selection criterion?
quiz.a: Without it, applications maintain indexes with separate writes, and crashes leave data and index permanently inconsistent.

title: TTL: automatic expiry
body: TTL, time to live, is automatic expiry of data after a set duration. Once the TTL passes, the store deletes the record without any cleanup job. TTLs are the simplest way to enforce short retention: session data, caches, temporary files and raw events can expire on schedule. They make deletion the default rather than a task someone must remember, and they cap how much data can accumulate.
deeper: The Part 2 retention modifier says short retention favours TTL-based stores. The design-doc Lifecycle section includes TTLs alongside tiering rules, archival and deletion. The anti-pattern 'retention by nobody' is defined partly by the absence of a TTL: no TTL, no lifecycle rule, no owner. TTLs also support the defaults mental model: if a platform gives new datasets a sensible TTL by default, the cheap, safe outcome happens when teams do nothing. In LSM stores, expired data is physically removed during compaction.

quiz.q: How do TTLs help avoid the 'retention by nobody' anti-pattern?
quiz.a: They make expiry automatic, so data is deleted on schedule without anyone needing to own a cleanup job.

title: Two-phase commit: atomic across participants
body: Two-phase commit is a protocol for atomic commit across multiple participants, such as several shards or databases. In the first phase, a coordinator asks every participant to prepare and promise it can commit. In the second, if all agreed, it tells them to commit; otherwise, to abort. The result is all-or-nothing across participants, at the cost of extra round trips and blocking if the coordinator fails.
deeper: Two-phase commit is how distributed SQL systems provide multi-shard transactions, and why the Part 2 flowchart treats 'need multi-row transactions or joins' as a major branch. The cost grows with distance: across regions, each phase pays a long round trip, which is why the chapter's design-doc example lists cross-region transactions as a typical non-goal. A crashed coordinator can leave participants waiting in the prepared state, so production systems replicate the coordinator's decision with consensus.

quiz.q: Why do many designs list cross-region transactions as a non-goal?
quiz.a: Atomic commit across regions needs protocols like two-phase commit whose round trips add large latency and complexity.

title: The core canon: papers, books and conferences to follow
body: The chapter's further reading lists the core storage canon. Papers include GFS (SOSP 2003), Bigtable (OSDI 2006), Ceph (OSDI 2006), Dynamo (SOSP 2007), Haystack (OSDI 2010), Windows Azure Storage (SOSP 2011), Spanner (OSDI 2012), f4 (OSDI 2014), Aurora (SIGMOD 2017), Tectonic (FAST 2021) and DynamoDB (USENIX ATC 2022). Recommended books are Kleppmann's Designing Data-Intensive Applications and Petrov's Database Internals. Conferences to follow are FAST, OSDI, SOSP, ATC, VLDB and SIGMOD.
deeper:
More papers in the list: Erasure Coding in Windows Azure Storage (USENIX ATC 2012), TAO (USENIX ATC 2013), Scaling Memcache at Facebook (NSDI 2013), FoundationDB Record Layer (SIGMOD 2019), DELF on deletion correctness (USENIX Security 2020), ShardStore (SOSP 2021) on formal methods for an Amazon S3 storage node, and the original Log-Structured Merge-Tree paper by O'Neil et al. (1996).

Blogs and data: Google's 'A peek behind Colossus' (2021), Dropbox's 'Inside the Magic Pocket' (2016), Backblaze drive stats for real disk failure rates, and the AWS Builders' Library on cells, shuffle sharding and retries.

Books: Kleppmann's book (O'Reilly, first edition 2017, with a second edition with Chris Riccomini) is called the best single book on replication, partitioning and storage engines. Petrov's Database Internals (2019) covers B-trees, LSM trees and consensus in depth. The Site Reliability Engineering book (2016) is free online, with its data-integrity chapter recommended. Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces explains file systems, RAID and crash consistency.

quiz.q: Which book does the chapter call the best single book on replication, partitioning and storage engines?
quiz.a: Martin Kleppmann's Designing Data-Intensive Applications (O'Reilly, first edition 2017).

title: Key takeaways: shape first, repair fast, count objects
body: The chapter's first four takeaways. Start from data shape and access pattern, not product names; the same app needs several stores. Durability comes from fast, parallel repair as much as from copy count; halving repair time helps as much as adding redundancy. Metadata, not bytes, is usually what breaks first, so count objects, not only terabytes. Defaults are policy, so make the safe, cheap choice the one teams get by doing nothing.
deeper:
Each takeaway compresses a mental model into a habit. 'Shape first' is the Part 2 flowchart and the Part 3 reference architecture, where profiles, photos, messages, logs and analytics each get a different store; the common mistake of one database for everything is its violation.

'Repair fast' is the durability model: loss needs extra failures inside the repair window, and that probability scales with the window squared for 3-way replication. Parallel repair, as in Dropbox's Magic Pocket, is the practical lever.

'Count objects' comes from GFS and HDFS hitting single-master metadata limits and from the small-file problem: a million 1 KB files cost far more metadata than one 1 GB file.

'Defaults are policy' comes from the observation that most teams keep whatever the platform does by default, illustrated by AWS making S3 encryption at rest the default in 2023. In reviews, the question is always: what happens if the team does nothing, and is that safe and cheap?

quiz.q: What does the chapter mean by 'defaults are policy'?
quiz.a: Most teams keep whatever the platform does by default, so the default effectively decides behaviour for most data; make the safe, cheap option the default.

title: Key takeaways: bound blast radius, plan exits, write deletion first
body: The remaining takeaways. Limit blast radius with cells or stamps, but know that smaller units strand capacity. Every system will be migrated, so build in abstraction, CDC, versions and open formats from day one. Deletion and migration are the two design-doc sections most often missing, so write them first. Interview answers and real designs share one shape: requirements, estimates, design, failure modes and trade-offs.
deeper:
Blast radius versus stranded capacity is a genuine trade-off, not a rule: Azure chose stamps to bound failure while Meta chose large Tectonic clusters to use capacity, and the chapter says both were right for their constraints.

The migration takeaway lists four concrete tools. An abstraction layer lets you swap engines behind a stable API, as Netflix's KV layer does. CDC lets a new store be filled and kept in sync. Record versions or timestamps let dual writes and backfills be reconciled. Open formats such as Parquet and Iceberg let new engines read old data without rewriting it.

Writing deletion and migration first reflects their cost curve: easy on day one, very hard in year three.

The final takeaway ties the practice problems to real work. The same five-part structure appears in the design-doc checklist, the design-review questions and the way to present a storage decision, so practising interview answers trains the same judgment used in production.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter say to write the deletion and migration sections of a design doc first?
quiz.a: They are the sections most often missing, and both are cheap to build into the design on day one but very hard to add in year three.
